Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 13, verse 1:

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Surat al-Ra'd is Meccan according to the view of al-Hasan, 'Ikrimah, 'Ata' and Jabir, and Medinan according to the view of al-Kalbi and Muqatil. Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah said: it is Medinan except for two verses in it which were revealed in Mecca, and they are His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And if only there was a Qur'an by which the mountains could be moved﴾ [al-Ra'd: 31] [to the end of the two verses]. [[The addition is from Tafsir al-Bahr.]]

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Al-Mar. These are the verses of the Book, and that which has been revealed to you from your Lord is the truth, but most of the people do not believe. (1)

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Al-Mar. These are the verses of the Book﴾. The discussion of these letters has already preceded.

(And that which has been revealed to you) meaning: and this Qur'an which has been revealed to you.

(from your Lord is the truth) not as the polytheists say: that you bring it from your own accord. So hold fast to it and act by what is in it. Muqatil said: it was revealed when the polytheists said: "Muhammad brought the Qur'an from his own accord."

"Alladhi" is in the nominative position, either as a conjunction with "ayat" or as a beginning (mubtada'), and "al-haqq" is its predicate (khabar). It is also permissible that its position be genitive, on the estimate: "and the ayat of that which has been revealed to you," and the nominative of "al-haqq" in this case is by an implied subject (mubtada' muqaddar), its estimate being: "that is the truth," like His saying: ﴿And they know. The truth﴾ [al-Baqarah: 146-147], meaning: that truth. Al-Farra' said: if you wish, you may make "alladhi" genitive as an adjective (na't) of "al-Kitab," even though the conjunction (wa) is in it, as one says: "This Book came to us from Abu Hafs and al-Faruq," and from it is the saying of the poet:

To the lordly king (al-qarm) and the son of the brave, and the lion of the battalion in the crowd [[Al-qarm (with fathah on the qaf): the lord; al-kataybah: the army; al-muzdahim: the place of crowding.]]

He means: to the lordly king, son of the brave, lion of the battalion.

(But most of the people do not believe).

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 13, verse 2:

Allah's words: "Allah is He who raised the heavens without pillars that you can see, then established Himself upon the Throne, and subjected the sun and the moon, each running to a specified term. He manages the affair and details the signs, so that you may be certain of meeting your Lord." (2)

Allah's words: ﴿Allah is He who raised the heavens without pillars that you can see﴾, and so on. When Allah made clear that the Qur'an is the truth, He made clear that the One who sent it down is able to bring about perfection. So look into His creations so that you may know the completeness of His power. This meaning has already been mentioned. Regarding His words "without pillars that you can see" there are two opinions. The first is that they are raised without pillars that you can see; this was said by Qatadah, Iyas ibn Mu'awiyah and others. The second is that they do have pillars, but we do not see them. Ibn 'Abbas said: they have pillars upon Mount Qaf. It may be said on this view that the pillars are His power by which He holds the heavens and the earth, and it is not visible to us; this was mentioned by al-Zajjaj. Ibn 'Abbas also said: the pillars are the faith of the believer. The heaven was ready to split apart because of the disbelief of the disbeliever; this was mentioned by al-Ghaznawi. The word "'amad" is the plural of "'amud" (pillar). al-Nabigha said:

"And I subjected the jinn to me, for I have permitted them
to build Tadmur with slabs and pillars." [[Another reading: "wa-khabbar al-jinn". Khayyis: subdued. Tadmur: a town in Syria, built by our master Sulayman, peace be upon him. Al-sifah: broad thin stones. 'Amad: plural of 'amud.]]

(Then He established Himself upon the Throne) The discussion of this has already passed. [[See vol. 7, p. 219.]]

(And subjected the sun and the moon) That is, He made them subservient for the benefit of His creation and the welfare of His servants, and every creature is subservient to the Creator.

(Each running to a specified term) That is, to a known time, which is the end of this world and the coming of the Hour, when the sun will be wound up, the moon will be eclipsed, the stars will be scattered, and the planets will be dispersed. Ibn 'Abbas said: by "the specified term" he meant their degrees and stations at which they arrive and beyond which they do not pass. It was also said: the meaning of "the specified term" is that the moon completes its orbit in a month and the sun in a year.

(He manages the affair) That is, He directs it as He wills.

(He details the signs) That is, He makes them clear. Whoever has power over these things has power over the restoration. For this reason He said: (so that you may be certain of meeting your Lord).

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 13, verse 3:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And it is He who spread out the earth﴾. When He had shown the signs of the heavens, He showed the signs of the earth. That is, He spread the earth lengthwise and widthwise.

(And He placed in it firm mountains) That is, mountains that are fixed. Its singular is *rasiyah* (a firmly set mountain), because the earth is anchored (*tarsu*) by them, meaning it becomes steady. *Al-irsa'* means firm settling. Antarah said:

*So I endured, steadfast in that, while the coward's soul looks up in fear.*
[[Before the verse:

*I knew that my death, if it comes to me, the swiftest flight will not save me from it.*]]

Jamil said:

*I love her, and by Him who set firm its foundations, a love which, when its signs appear outwardly, turns inward.*

Ibn Abbas and Ata said: The first mountain placed upon the earth was Abu Qubays.
[[Abu Qubays: a mountain overlooking the Sacred Mosque in Makkah.]]

Question: This verse refutes those who claim the earth is spherical like a ball, and refutes those who claim the earth's gates fall upon it. Ibn al-Rawandi claimed that beneath the earth there is a body that rises like the rising wind, while the falling body descends; so the falling and the rising are balanced in mass and force, and they are in agreement. Others claimed that the earth is composed of two bodies, one descending and the other ascending, and they balanced each other, and therefore it stood still. What the Muslims and the People of the Book (Jews and Christians) hold is that the earth stands still, remains at rest, and is spread out, and that its movement occurs only, as is customary, through an earthquake that strikes it.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And rivers﴾, that is, flowing waters in the earth, in which there are benefits for creation.

(And from all fruits He placed in it two mates, two kinds) Meaning two types. Abu Ubayda said: *zawj* is one, and it may be two (*ithnayn*). Al-Farra' said: By "two mates" here he means the male and the female, but this contradicts the text. It was also said: The meaning of "two mates" is two kinds, such as sweet and sour, dry and fresh, white and black, small and large.

(Indeed in that are signs) That is, indications and evidences (for a people who reflect).

There are five issues in this verse.

The first concerns His saying, ﴿And in the earth are neighbouring tracts﴾. There is an omission in the speech. The meaning is: "And in the earth are neighbouring tracts and non-neighbouring tracts," as He said, "garments that protect you from the heat" [see vol. 10, p. 159 onward], meaning "and that protect you from the cold," and the omitted part was dropped because the listener already knows it. The "neighbouring" tracts are the cities and what is inhabited, and the "non-neighbouring" are the deserts and what is uninhabited.

The second concerns His saying, ﴿neighbouring﴾, that is, villages close to one another, whose soil is one and whose water is one, containing crops and gardens, yet they differ in their fruits and dates. Some are sweet and some sour. Even a single branch of a tree may bear fruit that differs in size, colour and taste, though the sun and moon shine on all of them in one order. In this is the clearest proof of His oneness and the greatness of His self-sufficiency, and guidance for whoever has strayed from knowing Him. By His saying, ﴿watered with one water﴾, He drew attention to the fact that all of this is only by His will and purpose, and that it is subject to His power. This is the clearest proof against the claim of nature (al-tab', the idea that things act by their own inherent nature), for if it were by the water and the soil alone, with nature as the agent, the difference would not have occurred. It has also been said that the argument is that He established differences between the plots: some soil is sweet and some is brackish, even though they are adjacent. This too is one of the signs of the completeness of His power, exalted is He above what the wrongdoers and deniers say, to a great exaltation.

The third concerns the disbelievers, may Allah curse them, who held that every occurrence happens of itself without a maker. They claimed this about the fruits that come out of trees. They acknowledged that these things come into being, but denied that there is one who brings them into being, and they denied accidents (al-a'rad, attributes that inhere in substances). Another group said that the fruits come into being without a maker, but they affirmed an agent for accidents. The proof that what comes into being must have a bringer-into-being is that it comes into being at a particular time, and something of the same kind comes into being at another time. If its coming into being at its own time were due to its being particular to that time, then everything of its kind would have to come into being at that time. When it is shown that its being particular to that time is not necessary, it follows that its being particular to that time is due to a specifier who specified it. Were it not for His specifying it, its coming into being at that time would not be more fitting than its coming into being before or after. The full treatment of this belongs to the science of kalam (theology).

The fourth concerns His saying, ﴿and gardens of vines﴾. Al-Hasan read "wa-jannatin" with a kasra on the ta', as a construction meaning "and He placed in it gardens," which is governed by His saying, "and He placed in it firm mountains." It is also permissible for it to be in the genitive, taken as dependent on "kull" (every), meaning "and of every fruit, and of gardens." The rest read "jannatun" with a damma, meaning "and between them are gardens."

As for His saying, ﴿and crops and palm trees, clustered and non-clustered﴾, in the nominative: Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Hafs read it in the nominative as a conjunction with "gardens," that is, "and in the earth are crops and palm trees." The rest read it in the genitive as a continuation of "vines," so that the crops and palm trees are among the gardens. It is also permissible for it to be connected to "kull," as was explained regarding "wa-jannatun." Mujahid, al-Sulami and others read "sunwanun" with a damma on the sad, while the rest read it with a kasra. Both are dialectal variants, and both are the plural of sinw, which refers to a few palm trees, or two palm trees, gathered from one root, from which heads branch out and become palms. Its parallel is qinwan, whose singular is qinw. Abu Ishaq narrated from al-Bara', who said: "Sinwan is the clustered, and ghayr sinwan is the scattered." Al-Nahhas said: "This is also its meaning in the language. It is said of a palm when there is another palm or more with it, sinwan." Sinw means "like" or "twin," and from it is the words of the Prophet ﷺ: "A man's paternal uncle is the sinw of his father." There is no difference in it between the dual and the plural, nor in its inflection, so the nun of the plural is inflected and the nun of the dual is given a kasra. The poet said:

Knowledge and forbearance are two companions of nobility
for a man, an adornment when they are combined.
Twins whose beauty is not completed
except by gathering both of them together.

The fifth concerns His saying, ﴿watered with one water﴾, like the righteous and the wicked among the children of Adam: their father is one. This was said by al-Nahhas and al-Bukhari. 'Asim and Ibn 'Amir read "yusqa" with a ya', meaning "that all of that is watered." The rest read it with a ta', in agreement with "gardens." Abu Hatim and Abu 'Ubayda preferred this. Abu 'Amr said: "The feminine is better, because of His saying, 'and We favour some of them over others in the fruit,' and He did not say 'some of it.'" Hamza, al-Kisa'i and others read "wa-yufaddilu" with a ya', in response to His saying, "He arranges the affair" [al-Ra'd: 2], "He details the signs" [al-Ra'd: 2] and "He covers the night" [al-Ra'd: 3]. The rest read it with a nun, meaning "and We favour."

Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah narrated: "I heard the Prophet ﷺ say to 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him: 'People are of various trees, and you and I are of one tree.'" Then the Prophet ﷺ recited, "And in the earth are neighbouring tracts," until he reached His saying, "watered with one water." "Al-Ukul" means the fruit. Ibn 'Abbas said: "It means the sweet, the sour, the Persian [dates] and the dagl [poor-quality dates]." The Persian is a fine type of date, named after Persia. Dagl means inferior dates. It was also transmitted with a traced chain (marfu') from the hadith of Abu Hurayra that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, concerning His saying, "and We favour some of them over others in the fruit," said: "The Persian, the dagl, the sweet and the sour." Al-Tha'labi mentioned it. Al-Hasan said: "The purpose of this verse is a parable that Allah struck for the children of Adam. Their origin is one, yet they differ in good and evil, in faith and disbelief, just as the fruits differ though they are watered with one water." From this is the saying of the poet:

People are like plants, and plants are of many colours:
among them are trees of sandalwood, camphor and ban,
and among them are trees that yield resin all the years.

"Indeed in that are signs for a people who use reason": that is, indeed there are signs for whoever has a heart that understands from Allah, exalted is He.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 13, verse 5:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And if you are astonished, then astonishing is their saying﴾, meaning: if you are astonished, O Muhammad, at their denial of you after you were among them the truthful and trustworthy one, then more astonishing than that is their denial of resurrection. Allah, exalted is He, does not feel astonishment, and astonishment is not permissible for Him, because ʿajab (astonishment) is a change of the self caused by hidden causes [[In al-Jumal, on the authority of al-Qurtubi: ʿajab is a change of the self caused by hidden causes, and that is impossible with regard to Allah, exalted is He.]], and He mentioned it only so that His Prophet and the believers would be astonished by it. It was also said that the meaning is: if you are astonished, O Muhammad, at their denial of the return (resurrection) while they acknowledge that I am the Creator of the heavens and the earth and of the varied fruits from the one earth, then their saying is a matter at which creation marvels, because the return is in meaning the same as the initial creation. It was also said: the verse concerns those who deny the Creator, meaning: if you are astonished at their denial of the Maker despite the clear proofs that what changes must have a changer, then that is the object of astonishment. The wording of the verse indicates both the first and the second meanings, through His saying: ﴿When we are dust, shall we indeed be [raised] in a new creation?﴾, meaning: shall we be resurrected when we have become dust?

(﴿Shall we indeed be in a new creation?﴾) It is also read as "innā" (with the hamzah of assertion). ﴿Al-aghlal﴾ (the shackles) is the plural of ghull, which is a collar by which the hand is bound to the neck, meaning they will be shackled on the Day of Resurrection, as evidenced by His saying: ﴿When the shackles are around their necks﴾ [Ghafir: 71] up to His saying: ﴿Then in the Fire they will be burned﴾ [Ghafir: 72]. It was also said: the shackles are their evil deeds, which cling to them.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 13, verses 6–7:**

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿They ask you to hasten the evil before the good﴾. That is, because of their intense denial and rejection, they seek the punishment. It has been said that this refers to their saying: ﴿O Allah, if this is indeed the truth from You, then rain down on us stones from the sky﴾ [al-Anfal: 32]. [See vol. 7, p. 398.] Qatadah said: "They asked for the punishment before the well-being." Allah, glorified is He, has decreed that the punishment for this Ummah be delayed until the Day of Resurrection. It has also been said that "before the good" means before faith, through which security and good deeds are hoped for.

*Al-mathulat* (المَثُلاتُ) means punishments; its singular is *mathulah* (مَثُلَةٌ). It is narrated from al-A'mash (may Allah have mercy on him) that he read *al-muthulat* (الْمُثُلَاتُ) with a *damma* on the *mim* and a sukun on the *tha*, and this is the plural of *muthlah*. It is also permissible to read *al-mathulat* (المَثُلاتُ), with the *damma* replaced by a *fatha* because of its heaviness. It has also been said that the *fatha* is given in place of the *ha'* (of the singular). It is narrated from al-A'mash that he read *al-mathlat* (المَثْلَاتُ) with a *fatha* on the *mim* and a sukun on the *tha*; this is the plural of *mathlah*, and the *damma* was then dropped because of its heaviness. All of this was mentioned by al-Nahhas (may Allah have mercy on him). According to the reading of the majority, its singular is *mathulah* (مَثُلَةٌ), like *sadaqah* [and *sudqah*] [from manuscript ا]. The Tamim tribe pronounces both the *tha* and the *mim* with a *damma*, and according to their dialect the singular is *muthlah* (مُثْلَةٌ), with a *damma* on the *mim* and a sukun on the *tha*, like *ghurfah* and *ghurufat*. The verb from it is *mathaltu bihi, amthulu mathlan* (مَثَلْتُ بِهِ أَمْثُلُ مَثْلًا), with a *fatha* on the *mim* and a sukun on the *tha*.

﴿And indeed your Lord is full of forgiveness﴾, that is, He is forgiving toward the polytheists if they believe, and toward the sinners if they repent. Ibn 'Abbas said: "The most hopeful verse in the Book of Allah, the Exalted, is ﴿And indeed your Lord is full of forgiveness for mankind despite their wrongdoing﴾."

﴿And indeed your Lord is severe in punishment﴾, that is, if they persist in disbelief. Hammad ibn Salamah narrated from 'Ali ibn Zayd, from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, who said: When the verses ﴿And indeed your Lord is full of forgiveness for mankind despite their wrongdoing﴾ and ﴿And indeed your Lord is severe in punishment﴾ were revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "If it were not for Allah's pardon, His mercy and His overlooking, no one would enjoy a pleasant life; and if it were not for His retribution, His threat and His punishment, every person would become complacent."

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And those who disbelieve say: "Why has no sign been sent down to him from his Lord?"﴾, that is, why has it not been sent down? When they proposed signs and demanded them, Allah the Exalted said to His Prophet (ﷺ): ﴿You are only a warner﴾, that is, a teacher.

﴿And for every people there is a guide﴾, that is, a prophet who calls them to Allah. It has also been said that the guide is Allah; meaning, your duty is only to warn, and Allah is the guide of every people if He wills their guidance.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 13, verses 8–9:

There are eight issues in this passage.

The first concerns the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Allah knows what every female bears﴾, meaning male or female, beautiful or ugly, righteous or wicked. It has already been mentioned in the commentary on Surah al-An'am [[See vol. 7, p. 1 onwards.]] that Allah, glorified is He, alone possesses the knowledge of the unseen, with no partner. There I also mentioned the hadith of al-Bukhari from Ibn 'Umar that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The keys of the unseen are five," and the hadith goes on. In it: "No one knows what the wombs diminish except Allah." The scholars differed over the interpretation of the words: (and what the wombs diminish and what they increase). Qatadah said: the meaning is what miscarries before the nine months, and what increases beyond the nine months. Ibn 'Abbas also said likewise. Mujahid said: when a woman menstruates during her pregnancy, that is a deficiency in her child; if she exceeds nine months, it is a completion of what was lacking. It is also reported from him that the "diminishing" is what the wombs reduce of blood, and the "increase" is what they add of it. It was also said: the diminishing and the increase refer to the child, such as the loss of a finger or something else, or the addition of a finger or something else. It was said: the diminishing is the cessation of menstrual blood, and the "increase" is postpartum bleeding (nifas) after delivery.

The second issue: this verse is evidence that a pregnant woman may menstruate. This is the position of Malik and one of the two opinions of al-Shafi'i. 'Ata', al-Sha'bi and others said that she does not menstruate, and Abu Hanifah held the same view, using this verse as evidence. Ibn 'Abbas, in interpreting it, said: it refers to the menstruation of pregnant women. The same is narrated from 'Ikrimah and Mujahid, and it is the view of 'A'ishah, who used to rule for pregnant women who menstruated that they should abandon the prayer. The Companions were numerous at that time, and none of them objected to her, so it became like a consensus (ijma', scholarly agreement), as stated by Ibn al-Qassar. [[In the first edition: "qalahu Ibn 'Abbas qala Ibn al-Qassar." The wording of the originals is not like that, so we have deleted it.]] It is also mentioned that two men disputed over a child, and they brought their case to 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him. He presented the child to the qafah (tracking experts who identify lineage by physical resemblance), and the qafah attributed the child to both of them. 'Umar struck them with a dirrah (a whip). He then asked some women of Quraysh, saying: "Look into this child's matter." They said: "The first man was alone with her and left her, and she menstruated while pregnant, so she thought her waiting period had ended. Then the second man entered upon her, and the child grew through the second man's water." 'Umar said: "Allahu Akbar!" and attributed the child to the first man. He did not say that a pregnant woman does not menstruate, and none of the Companions said so, so this shows it is a consensus. And Allah knows best. The opponent argued: if a pregnant woman menstruates, and whatever blood a woman sees is menstruation, then the istibra' (the waiting period to establish a slave-woman is not pregnant) by menstruation would not be valid, and this is a consensus. It is narrated from Malik in the Kitab Muhammad what suggests that it is not menstruation.

The third issue: this verse is evidence that a pregnant woman may deliver her child in less than nine months or more. The scholars agreed that the minimum period of pregnancy is six months, and that 'Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan was born after six months.

The fourth issue: these six months are reckoned by the lunar months, like all the months of the Shari'ah. For this reason, it is narrated in the school of Malik, from some of Malik's companions, and I think it is in the book of Ibn Harith, that if it falls short of the six months by three days, the child is still attributed to the husband, because of the deficiency and excess of the months. Ibn 'Atiyyah related this.

The fifth issue: the scholars differed over the maximum period of pregnancy. Ibn Juraij narrated from Jamilah bint Sa'd, from 'A'ishah, who said: pregnancy may last more than two years, as long as it takes for the shadow of the spindle to move. This was reported by al-Daraqutni. Jamilah bint Sa'd, the sister of 'Ubayd ibn Sa'd, and (from al-Layth ibn Sa'd) said: its maximum is three years. From al-Shafi'i it is reported as four years. It is reported from Malik in one of his two narrations, while the well-known view from him is five years. Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 13, verse 10:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿It is the same whether any of you conceals speech or speaks it aloud﴾. "Concealing speech" is what a person says to himself, and "speaking aloud" is what he says to others. The meaning is that Allah, glorified is He, knows what a person conceals of good and evil, just as He knows what he speaks aloud of good and evil.

"Minkum" (of you) may be a description of "sawa'" (equal/same). The implied sense is: the secret of one who conceals and the open speech of one who speaks aloud are equal, of you. It may also be linked to "sawa'" in the sense of: "it is equal (yastawi) for you," like your saying: "I passed by Zayd." It may also be read with the implied sense: the secret of whoever among you conceals and the open speech of whoever among you speaks aloud. It may also be read with the implied sense: "one who is equal (dhu sawa')" among you is whoever conceals speech and whoever speaks it aloud, just as you say: "the justice (adl) of Zayd and 'Amr," meaning "the two who are just (dhawa adl)." It has also been said: "sawa'" means "equal" (mustawin), so there is no need to posit an omitted noun.

﴿And whoever is hidden by the night and goes freely by day﴾. That is, the secret and the open are equal in the knowledge of Allah, as are the one who appears on the roads and the one who hides in the darkness. Al-Akhfash and Qutrub said: "al-mustakhfi bi'l-layl" means the one who is visible. From this comes "khafaytu al-shay'" and "akhfaytuhu," meaning I made it appear, and "akhfaytu al-shay'" meaning I extracted it. From this, the grave-robber is called "al-mukhtafi." Imru' al-Qays said:

They were brought out from their tunnels (anfaq, plural of nafaq: a passage in the earth leading to another place; he uses it for the hole of the mouse) as though / the rain-cloud of an evening, loud-voiced (mujallab), brought them forth (khafahunna)

"Al-sarib" is the one who is concealed, i.e., the one who enters a passage (sarab). From this is the saying: "the wild animal slipped away (insaraba)" when it entered its lair. Ibn 'Abbas said: "mustakhfin" means hidden, and "sarib" means manifest. Mujahid said: "mustakhfin" means hidden in sins, and "sarib" means openly. It has also been said that the meaning of "sarib" is going away. Al-Kisa'i said: "sariba yasribu sarban wa surubban" means he went away. A poet said (he is al-Akhnas ibn Shihab al-Taghlibi, meaning that the people stayed in one place, not daring to move, and they held back their stallion from advancing, so their camels followed him out of fear that he would be raided; while we, being mighty, unfastened the tether of our stallion so that he might go wherever he wished):

And every people who have stayed by the tether of their stallion, while we have loosed its tether, so it is free to roam (sarib)

That is, going away. Abu Raja' said: "al-sarib" is the one who goes on his face across the earth. A poet said (he is Qays ibn al-Khatim, and the rest of the verse is: "and dreams draw near though they are not near"):

Where have you gone, though you were not one who wanders

Al-Qutabi said: "sarib bi'l-nahar" means one who goes about his needs swiftly, from their saying: "the water flowed away (insaraba al-ma')." Al-Asma'i said: "khalla sarbahu" means his path.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (*al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran*) on surah 13, verse 11:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿For him there are successive angels﴾, meaning: for Allah there are angels who follow one another by night and by day. When the angels of the night ascend, the angels of the day follow them. He said "mu'aqqibat" (successive), although the angels are masculine, because it is the plural of mu'aqqiba (feminine form). One says malak mu'aqqib (a male angel who follows), and malaika mu'aqqiba (angels who follow), and then mu'aqqibat is the plural of the plural. Some of them read: "lahu ma'aqib min bayni yadayhi wa min khalfihi." Ma'aqib is the plural of mu'aqqib [[Al-Zamakhshari said: it is the plural of mu'aqqib or mu'aqqiba with the qaf doubled in both, and the ya' is a substitute for dropping one of the two qafs in the broken plural. Ibn Jinni said: it is a broken plural of mu'aqqib, like mut'im and mata'im, as if it was pluralised as mu'aqqiba, then the ha' was dropped from the plural and the ya' was substituted for it. Al-Alusi said: and perhaps this is the most apparent. (Ruh al-Ma'ani)]]. It was also said that the angels are called mu'aqqiba in accordance with the wording "malaika." It was also said: it is feminine because of how much this occurs among them, like nassaba, allama and rawiya. Al-Jawhari and others said this. Ta'aqqub means returning after beginning, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿and he turned back, not looking behind him﴾ [al-Naml: 10], meaning he did not return. In the hadith [[The hadith concerns supplication. Its full text is in Sahih Muslim: "Mu'aqqibat, whoever says them will not be disappointed, after every obligatory prayer: thirty-three tasbih, thirty-three tahmid, and thirty-four takbir." They were called mu'aqqibat because they are repeated again and again, or because they are said after every prayer.]]: "Mu'aqqibat, whoever says them, or does them, will not be disappointed," and he mentioned tasbih, tahmid and takbir. Abu al-Haytham said: they were called "mu'aqqibat" because they recur time after time. The doer of an action who then returns to it has done ta'qib (followed up). The mu'aqqibat among camels are those that stand behind the camels that are fighting over the watering trough; when one camel leaves, another enters its place. As for his saying, "min bayni yadayhi," it refers to the one who hides by night and the one who moves openly by day.

﴿They guard him by the command of Allah﴾. Scholars differed about this guarding. It was said: it may be that the angels are appointed over them to protect them from wild animals, poisonous creatures and harmful things, out of Allah's kindness towards them. But when the decree comes, they leave him to it. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with them both. Abu Mijlaz said: a man from Murad [[Murad (with a damma on the m, and a final unpointed dal): a tribe of the Arabs named after its father.]] came to 'Ali and said: "Be on your guard, for some people from Murad want to kill you." He said: "With every man are two angels who guard him, so long as it has not been decreed. When the decree comes, they leave him between himself and the decree of Allah. The term is a fortified fortress."

According to this, "they guard him by the command of Allah" means by the command of Allah and with His permission, so "min" has the meaning of "bi" (with), and prepositions may stand in place of one another. It was also said that "min" has the meaning of "'an" (from), meaning they guard him from the command of Allah; this is close to the first meaning, that is, their guarding is from Allah's command and not from their own selves. This is the saying of al-Hasan. You say: "kasawtuhu 'an 'uri" and "min 'uri" (I clothed him from nakedness), and from it is the Exalted's saying: ﴿who fed them against hunger﴾ [Quraysh: 4], meaning "'an ju'" (from hunger).

It was also said: they guard him from the angels of punishment, so that no punishment befalls him, because Allah does not change the blessing and wellbeing of a people until they change what is in themselves by persisting in disbelief. If they persist, the appointed term arrives, the vengeance descends upon them, and the successive guardians leave them.

It was also said: they guard him from the jinn. Ka'b said: "Were it not that Allah has appointed over you angels who ward off from you at your eating and drinking and in your private parts, the jinn would snatch you away."

The angels of punishment are part of Allah's command, and He specified them by saying "from the command of Allah," because they are not seen, as He said: ﴿Say: The spirit is from the command of my Lord﴾ [al-Isra': 85], meaning it is not something you witness.

Al-Farra' said: there is inversion in the speech; its meaning is: "For him are successive angels from the command of Allah, from before him and from behind him, guarding him." This is narrated from Mujahid, Ibn Jurayj and al-Nakha'i. And according to the view that the angels of punishment and the jinn are from Allah's command, there is no inversion in it.

Ibn Jurayj said: the meaning is that they guard his deeds for him, and the word is elided (the genitive is omitted). Qatada said: they write down his sayings and his actions.

If the successive ones are the angels, it is permissible for the pronoun in "lahu" to refer to Allah, as we have mentioned. It is also permissible for it to refer to the one who hides. This is one view.

It was also said: "For him are successive angels from before him and from behind him" refers to the Prophet (ﷺ), meaning the angels guard him from his enemies. The Messenger was mentioned in His saying: ﴿Why has a sign not been sent down upon him from his Lord? You are only a warner﴾ [al-Ra'd: 7]. The meaning is: whether among you one speaks secretly or openly, it does not harm the Prophet (ﷺ); rather, for him are successive angels who guard him, peace be upon him. It is also permissible for this to refer to all the Messengers, because He said: ﴿and for every people there is a guide﴾ [al-Ra'd: 7], meaning they guard the guide from before him and from behind him.

A fourth view: the verse refers to the sultans and rulers who have people before and behind them guarding them. When the command of Allah comes, they will not avail them against Allah in anything. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ikrima. Likewise al-Dahhak said: it is the sultan who takes precautions against the command of Allah, the polytheist.

It has been said that in the speech according to this interpretation there is an elided negation, its meaning being: they do not guard him from the command of Allah the Exalted. This was mentioned by al-Mawardi.

Al-Mahdawi said: whoever makes the successive ones to be the guards, the meaning is: they guard him from the command of Allah according to their assumption and claim.

It was also said: whether one speaks secretly or openly, he has guards and helpers who follow one another over him, and they urge him towards disobedience, and protect him from being affected by admonition. When this disobedient person changes what is in himself through prolonged persistence, that becomes a cause for punishment, so it is as if he is the one who brings the punishment upon himself. So His saying "they guard him from the command of Allah" means from complying with the command of Allah.

'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd said: the mu'aqqibat are what follows one another of the command of Allah the Exalted and His decree concerning His servants. Al-Mawardi said: whoever holds this view has two interpretations of His saying "they guard him from the command of Allah." One: they guard him from death, as long as the appointed term has not come; this was said by al-Dahhak. Two: they guard him from jinn and harmful vermin, as long as the decreed matter has not come; this was said by Abu Umama and Ka'b al-Ahbar. When the decreed matter comes, they leave him.

He said: "One angel on your right writes down the good deeds, and another on your left writes down the bad deeds. The one on the right is in charge of the one on the left. When you do a good deed, it is written as ten. When you do a bad deed, the one on the left says to the one on the right: 'Shall I write it?' He says: 'No, perhaps he will ask forgiveness of Allah the Exalted or repent to Him.' When he says it three times, he says: 'Yes, write it down. May Allah relieve us of him. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Not a word does he utter but that with him is a watcher, ready﴾ [Qaf: 18]. And two angels are in front of you and behind you. Allah the Exalted says: 'For him there are successive angels from before him and from behind him, guarding him by the command of Allah.' [And an angel holds your forelock. When you humble yourself before Allah, He raises you; when you act arrogantly against Allah, He breaks you. [[The addition is from Tafsir al-Tabari and others.]]] Two angels are on your lips, and they only guard for you the prayer upon Muhammad and his family. An angel stands over your mouth, not letting the snake enter your mouth. Two angels are over your eyes. These are ten angels for every human being, who take turns: the angels of the night with the angels of the day, because the angels of the night are not the angels of the day. This was mentioned by al-Tha'labi.

Al-Hasan said: the mu'aqqibat are four angels who gather at the time of the dawn prayer.

Al-Tabari's preference is that the mu'aqqibat are the escorts before and behind the rulers, and the pronoun in "lahu" refers to them, as already mentioned.

The scholars, may Allah be pleased with them, said: Allah the Exalted has made His commands in two ways. One: He decreed their descent and occurrence upon their owner. This no one can repel or change. The other: He decreed their coming, but did not decree their descent and occurrence; rather, He decreed their averting through repentance, supplication, charity and protection.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not change what is with a people until they change what is in themselves﴾. In this verse Allah the Exalted informs that He does not change what is with a people until a change occurs from them, either from them, or from the observer of them, or from someone who is among them by cause, as Allah changed the fleeing ones on the day of Uhud because of the archers changing themselves, and other examples from the Shari'a. [[By wickedness (khabath) is meant immorality and depravity.]] And Allah knows best.

Wali and waliy are like qadir and qadir (both forms of the same pattern).

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 13, verses 12–13 (part 1 of 2):

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿It is He who shows you the lightning, as a fear and as a hope, and produces the heavy clouds﴾, that is, with rain. "Al-sahab" (the clouds) is a collective noun, its singular being "sahabah." Its plurals are also "suhub" and "sawahib."

It is also said that thunder is an angel seated on a throne between heaven and earth, with seventy thousand angels on his right and the same number on his left. When he turns to his right and glorifies, all of them glorify out of fear of Allah, and when he turns to his left and glorifies, all of them glorify out of fear of Allah.

﴿And He sends the thunderbolts and strikes with them whom He wills﴾.

Is He of silver, of iron or of copper?" The people were appalled by his words. He said: "I will answer Muhammad with a lord who does not know him!" The Prophet ﷺ sent to him several times, and he kept saying the same thing. While the group were disputing with him and calling him, a cloud rose and came over their heads. It thundered, flashed, and hurled a thunderbolt, which burned the disbeliever while they were sitting there. They returned to the Prophet ﷺ, and some of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ met them. They said: "Your companion has been burned." They asked: "How did you know?" They said: "Allah revealed it to the Prophet ﷺ." Then: ﴿and He sends the thunderbolts and strikes with them whom He wills﴾. Al-Tha'labi reported it from al-Hasan, and al-Qushayri reported its meaning from Anas, and it will come.

It is also said: the verse was revealed concerning Arbad ibn Rabi'ah, the brother of Labid ibn Rabi'ah, and concerning Amir ibn al-Tufayl. They entered the mosque. People were struck by Amir's beauty, though he was one-eyed, and he was one of the most handsome of men. A man from among the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ said: "O Messenger of Allah, this is Amir ibn al-Tufayl, who has come toward you." He said: "Leave him, for if Allah wills good for him, He will guide him." So he came and stood before him and said: "O Muhammad, what will I get if I become Muslim?" He said: "You will have what the Muslims have, and you will bear what the Muslims bear." He said: "Will you make the matter (of leadership) mine after you?" He said: "That is not up to me; it is up to Allah, who places it wherever He wills." He said: "Will you then make me over the rural folk while you are over the urban?" He said: "No." He said: "What then will you give me?" He said: "I will give you the reins of horses, with which you may fight in the way of Allah." He said: "Or do I not already have the reins of horses today? Stand with me and let me speak with you." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ stood with him. Amir had signalled to Arbad: "When you see me speaking with him, come up behind him and strike him with the sword." He began to argue with the Prophet ﷺ and dispute with him. Allah sent a thunderbolt upon him on a clear, hot day, and it burned him. Amir fled and said: "O Muhammad! You have prayed to your Lord against Arbad until you killed him. So Allah sent an angel who struck him with his wing and threw him into the dust, and a great swelling appeared on his knee at once. He returned to the house of the Salulite woman, saying: "A swelling like the swelling of a camel, and death in the house of a Salulite woman!" Then he mounted his horse and died on its back.

Labid ibn Rabi'ah lamented his brother Arbad and said:
"O eye, would that you had wept for Arbad, when we stood and the disputants stood in distress [[Kabad: hardship and toil.]]
I fear for Arbad the calamities, and I do not dread the rising of Simak or of Asad [[The stars.]]
The thunder and the thunderbolts with the horsemen bereaved me, on the day of the fearful, urgent battle [[Najd: quick to respond.]]"
And in the same poem he said:
"Surely the calamity is no calamity like it: the loss of a brother, like the light of a star.
O Arbad, of good nature, generous in his forefathers, you have left me walking with a broken horn [[A broken horn: broken.]]"
Labid became Muslim after that, may Allah be pleased with him.

Issue: Abu Hurayrah narrated... Abaan narrated from Anas, who said: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The thunderbolt does not strike one who remembers Allah, Mighty and Majestic." Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, said: whenever the Prophet ﷺ heard the sound of thunder he would say: "Glory be to Him whom the thunder glorifies with His praise and the angels out of fear of Him, and He is powerful over all things." If a thunderbolt strikes him, then I am responsible for his blood money [[There is a gap in the wording; what is in the tafsir of al-Baghawi is: from Ibn Abbas: whoever hears the sound of thunder and says... the hadith. Then he said: if a thunderbolt strikes him, then its blood money is upon me. Muhaqqiq.]]. Al-Khatib mentioned from the hadith of Sulayman ibn Ali ibn Abdullah ibn Abbas, from his father, from his grandfather, who said: we were with Umar on a journey, and thunder and hail struck us. Ka'b said to us: whoever says, when he hears the thunder: "Glory be to Him whom the thunder glorifies with His praise and the angels out of fear of Him," three times, will be spared from what happens in that thunder. We did so and were spared. Then I met Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, and a hailstone [[Al-barad (with a vowel on the 'a'): hail.]] had struck his nose and left a mark. I said: "O Commander of the Faithful, what is this?" He said: "A hailstone struck my nose and left a mark." I said: "Ka'b, when he heard the thunder, said to us: whoever says, when he hears the thunder, 'Glory be to Him whom the thunder glorifies with His praise and the angels out of fear of Him,' three times, will be spared from what happens in that thunder. We said it and were spared." Umar said: "Why did you not tell us so that we could say it too?" This meaning has already passed in al-Baqarah [[See vol. 1, p. 216 onward.]].

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿while they dispute concerning Allah﴾. That is, the dispute of the Jew when he asked about Allah the Exalted: "Of what is He made?" This was said by Mujahid. Ibn Jurayj said: it is the dispute of Arbad concerning his intention to kill the Prophet ﷺ. It may be that ﴿while they dispute concerning Allah﴾ is a circumstantial clause, and it may be that it is a new sentence. Anas narrated that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent to a notable of the polytheists, calling him to Allah, Mighty and Majestic. He said to the Messenger of Allah: "Tell me about this god of yours: is it of silver, of gold or of copper?" He was appalled by this. He returned to him and informed him. The Prophet said: "Go back to him and call him." He went back to him, and a thunderbolt had struck him. He returned to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and the verse had been revealed: ﴿while they dispute concerning Allah﴾.

﴿And He is severe in might﴾. Ibn al-A'rabi said: "al-mihal" means cunning, and cunning from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is disposing by means of the truth. Al-Nahhas said: cunning from Allah is delivering harm to the one who deserves it from a direction he does not perceive. Ibn al-Yazidi narrated from Abu Zayd: "He is severe in mihal," that is, in retribution. Al-Azhari said: "al-mihal" means strength and severity. "Al-mahl" is severity; the mim is original. One says: "I contended with so-and-so with mihal," meaning I contested with him until it became clear which of us was stronger. Abu Ubayd said: "al-mihal" means punishment and harm. Ibn Arafah said: "al-mihal" means dispute; it is said: "He did not budge from his command," meaning he argued. Al-Qutaybi said: that is, severe in plotting. Its root is from ḥīlah (stratagem), and its mim was made like the mim of place, and its root is from kawn, then one says: "I established myself (tamakkantu)." Al-Azhari said: Ibn Qutaybah erred in saying that the mim in it is extra; rather it is original. When you see a word of the pattern fi'āl whose first letter is a kasra-marked mim, it is original, such as mihād, milāk and mirās, and other letters. And mif'al, when it derives from triliteral roots, comes with the waw made explicit [[That is, the waw in roots with waw, and the yā’ in roots with yā’, as in al-mu'īr and al-muzīl, as in al-Lisan.]], such as mizwad, miḥwal and miḥwar, and other letters. [[That is, al-Azhari, as in al-Lisan, root m-ḥ-l.]] He also said: al-A'raj recited "wa-huwa shadīdu l-mihāl" with a fatḥah on the mim, and its interpretation on this reading came from Ibn Abbas as "al-ḥawl" (strength or power). Abu Ubayd al-Harawi mentioned all of this, except what we mentioned first from Ibn al-A'rabi. The sayings of the Companions and the Successors with the same meaning are eight: the first is "severe in enmity," said by Ibn Abbas. The second is "severe in power (ḥawl)," also said by Ibn Abbas. The third is "severe in seizing," said by Ali ibn Abi Talib. The fourth is "severe in rancour," said by Ibn Abbas. The fifth is "severe in strength," said by Mujahid. The sixth is "severe in anger," said by Wahb ibn Munabbih. The seventh is "severe in destruction by drought, which is famine," also said by al-Hasan. The eighth is "severe in stratagem," said by Qatadah. Abu Ubayda Ma'mar said: "al-mihal" and "al-mumahalah" mean contending in cunning and overpowering. He recited for al-A'sha:
"A shoot of nabk-wood swaying in the branch of glory, abundant in generosity, severe in might."
And another said [[He is Dhu al-Rummah, and the verse is from a qasidah praising Bilal ibn Abi Burdah ibn Abi Musa. "Al-labs" means confusion. "Al-shaghazib," said al-Asma'i, is a kind of stratagem in wrestling, which is that a man enters between the legs of his opponent and throws him down. The meaning: each man among the people prepared for him an argument and a plot.]]:
"He mixed among the people, and each of them prepared for him the shaghazib and the mihal."

Abd al-Muttalib said:

O Allah, indeed a man defends his household, so defend Your sanctuary-folk (ḥilālaka).
Let not their cross nor their cunning overcome Your cunning (miḥālaka) in the face of the enemy.

[Note: ḥilāl (with kasra): the people who dwell as neighbours, meaning the inhabitants of the Sacred Precinct. It is also narrated: ghadawā (the root ghadw, which is the day that comes after your day, its final letter having been dropped). Lisan. It is also narrated: abdā maḥālaka. Al-Bahr.]

Then he said: if a thunderbolt strikes him, then its blood money is upon me. Muhaqqiq.]]. Al-Khatib mentioned from the hadith of Sulayman ibn Ali ibn Abdullah ibn Abbas, from his father, from his grandfather, who said: we were with Umar on a journey, and thunder and hail struck us. Ka'b said to us: whoever says, when he hears the thunder: "Glory be to Him whom the thunder glorifies with His praise and the angels out of fear of Him," three times, will be spared from what happens in that thunder. We did so and were spared. Then I met Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, and a hailstone [[Al-barad (with a vowel on the 'a'): hail.]] had struck his nose and left a mark. I said: "O Commander of the Faithful, what is this?" He said: "A hailstone struck my nose and left a mark." I said: "Ka'b, when he heard the thunder, said to us: whoever says, when he hears the thunder, 'Glory be to Him whom the thunder glorifies with His praise and the angels out of fear of Him,' three times, will be spared from what happens in that thunder. We said it and were spared." Umar said: "Why did you not tell us so that we could say it too?" This meaning has already passed in al-Baqarah [[See vol. 1, p. 216 onward.]].

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿while they dispute concerning Allah﴾. That is, the dispute of the Jew when he asked about Allah the Exalted: "Of what is He made?" This was said by Mujahid. Ibn Jurayj said: it is the dispute of Arbad concerning his intention to kill the Prophet ﷺ. It may be that ﴿while they dispute concerning Allah﴾ is a circumstantial clause, and it may be that it is a new sentence. Anas narrated that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent to a notable of the polytheists, calling him to Allah, Mighty and Majestic. He said to the Messenger of Allah: "Tell me about this god of yours: is it of silver, of gold or of copper?" He was appalled by this. He returned to him and informed him. The Prophet said: "Go back to him and call him." He went back to him, and a thunderbolt had struck him. He returned to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and the verse had been revealed: ﴿while they dispute concerning Allah﴾.

﴿And He is severe in might﴾. Ibn al-A'rabi said: "al-mihal" means cunning, and cunning from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is disposing by means of the truth. Al-Nahhas said: cunning from Allah is delivering harm to the one who deserves it from a direction he does not perceive. Ibn al-Yazidi narrated from Abu Zayd: "He is severe in mihal," that is, in retribution. Al-Azhari said: "al-mihal" means strength and severity. "Al-mahl" is severity; the mim is original. One says: "I contended with so-and-so with mihal," meaning I contested with him until it became clear which of us was stronger. Abu Ubayd said: "al-mihal" means punishment and harm. Ibn Arafah said: "al-mihal" means dispute; it is said: "He did not budge from his command," meaning he argued. Al-Qutaybi said: that is, severe in plotting. Its root is from ḥīlah (stratagem), and its mim was made like the mim of place, and its root is from kawn, then one says: "I established myself (tamakkantu)." Al-Azhari said: Ibn Qutaybah erred in saying that the mim in it is extra; rather it is original. When you see a word of the pattern fi'āl whose first letter is a kasra-marked mim, it is original, such as mihād, milāk and mirās, and other letters. And mif'al, when it derives from triliteral roots, comes with the waw made explicit [[That is, the waw in roots with waw, and the yā’ in roots with yā’, as in al-mu'īr and al-muzīl, as in al-Lisan.]], such as mizwad, miḥwal and miḥwar, and other letters. [[That is, al-Azhari, as in al-Lisan, root m-ḥ-l.]] He also said: al-A'raj recited "wa-huwa shadīdu l-mihāl" with a fatḥah on the mim, and its interpretation on this reading came from Ibn Abbas as "al-ḥawl" (strength or power). Abu Ubayd al-Harawi mentioned all of this, except what we mentioned first from Ibn al-A'rabi. The sayings of the Companions and the Successors with the same meaning are eight: the first is "severe in enmity," said by Ibn Abbas. The second is "severe in power (ḥawl)," also said by Ibn Abbas. The third is "severe in seizing," said by Ali ibn Abi Talib. The fourth is "severe in rancour," said by Ibn Abbas. The fifth is "severe in strength," said by Mujahid. The sixth is "severe in anger," said by Wahb ibn Munabbih. The seventh is "severe in destruction by drought, which is famine," also said by al-Hasan. The eighth is "severe in stratagem," said by Qatadah. Abu Ubayda Ma'mar said: "al-mihal" and "al-mumahalah" mean contending in cunning and overpowering. He recited for al-A'sha:
"A shoot of nabk-wood swaying in the branch of glory, abundant in generosity, severe in might."
And another said [[He is Dhu al-Rummah, and the verse is from a qasidah praising Bilal ibn Abi Burdah ibn Abi Musa. "Al-labs" means confusion. "Al-shaghazib," said al-Asma'i, is a kind of stratagem in wrestling, which is that a man enters between the legs of his opponent and throws him down. The meaning: each man among the people prepared for him an argument and a plot.]]:
"He mixed among the people, and each of them prepared for him the shaghazib and the mihal."

Abd al-Muttalib said:

O Allah, indeed a man defends his household, so defend Your sanctuary-folk (ḥilālaka).
Let not their cross nor their cunning overcome Your cunning (miḥālaka) in the face of the enemy.

[Note: ḥilāl (with kasra): the people who dwell as neighbours, meaning the inhabitants of the Sacred Precinct. It is also narrated: ghadawā (the root ghadw, which is the day that comes after your day, its final letter having been dropped). Lisan. It is also narrated: abdā maḥālaka. Al-Bahr.]

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 13, verse 14:

His words, exalted is He: ﴿To Him is the call of truth﴾, meaning: to Allah belongs the call of truth (da'wat al-sidq). Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah and others said: it is "There is no god but Allah." Al-Hasan said: Allah is the Truth (al-Haqq), so His call is the call of truth. It was also said: sincerity in supplication is the call of truth; this was said by some later scholars. It was also said: the call of truth is supplicating Him at the time of fear, for in such a state none is called upon except Him, as He says: ﴿Those whom you call upon fall away from you except Him﴾ [al-Isra: 67]. Al-Mawardi said: this is closer to the context of the verse, because He said: (And those who call upon other than Him), meaning the idols and the images.

(They do not respond to them with anything) meaning: they do not respond to their supplication, nor do they hear their call.

(Except like one who stretches his hands out to water so that it may reach his mouth, but it does not reach it) Allah, exalted and mighty is He, struck the water as a parable for their despair of being answered in their supplication, because the Arabs use as a parable for one who strives for what he cannot attain the one who grasps water in his hand. He said:

So I became, regarding what was between me and her, of affection, like the one who grasps water in his hand.

There are three aspects to the meaning of this parable. The first: one who calls upon a god other than Allah is like the thirsty man who calls the water toward his mouth from afar, wishing to take it but unable to reach it with his tongue, and gestures toward it with his hand, but it never comes to him, because water does not respond, and water cannot reach him. This was said by Mujahid. The second: he is like the thirsty man who sees his reflection in the water, and has stretched his palm into it so that it may reach his mouth, but it does not reach it, because of the falseness of his assumption and the corruption of his imagining. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas. The third: he is like one who stretches his hand to the water in order to grasp it, but not a drop of it solidifies in his palm. Al-Farra' asserted that what is meant by "the water" here is the well, because it is the source of water, and that the parable is like one who extends his hand to the well without a rope. His witness is the poet's words:

Indeed the water is the water of my father and my grandfather, and the well, I dug it and I drew it.

'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, said: he is like the thirsty man at the lip of the well, who does not reach the bottom of the well, nor does the water rise up to him. The meaning of "Except like one who stretches" is: except like the response of one who stretches his hands "to the water"; the verbal noun is annexed to the one who stretches, then the annexed word is omitted, and the subject of the annexed verbal noun is implied in meaning, which is the water. The meaning is: except like the response of one who stretches his hands to the water. The lam in His words "so that it may reach his mouth" is connected to the stretching. His words "but it does not reach it" refer to the water: that is, the water does not reach his mouth. It is also permissible that "it" refers to the mouth: that is, the mouth does not reach the water.

(And the supplication of the disbelievers is only in error) meaning: the worship of the disbelievers of idols is only in error, because it is polytheism. It was also said: "only in error" means that this supplication strays from them, so they find no way to it, as He says: ﴿Where are those you used to call upon besides Allah? They will say: They have strayed from us﴾ [al-A'raf: 37]. Ibn 'Abbas said: that is, the voices of the disbelievers are veiled from Allah, so He does not hear their supplication.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 13, verse 15:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿To Allah prostrate whoever is in the heavens and the earth, willingly and unwillingly﴾. Al-Hasan, Qatadah and others said: the believer prostrates willingly, and the disbeliever prostrates unwillingly, by the sword. It is also related from Qatadah: the disbeliever prostrates unwillingly when faith will no longer benefit him. Al-Zajjaj said: the disbeliever's prostration is unwilling in that it contains submission and the mark of the made thing.

Ibn Zayd said: "willingly" refers to one who entered Islam out of desire, and "unwillingly" refers to one who entered it out of fear, by the sword. It was also said: "willingly" refers to one whose time in Islam has lengthened so that he has become accustomed to prostration, and "unwillingly" refers to one who compels his own self for the sake of Allah, the Exalted. On this view the verse concerns the believers, and "and the earth" means "and some of those on the earth." Al-Qushayri said: there are two approaches to the verse. The first is that it is general but intended as specific: the believer prostrates willingly, and some of the disbelievers prostrate under compulsion and fear, like the hypocrites, so the verse is applied to these; this was mentioned by al-Farra'. It was also said on this view: the verse concerns the believers, some of whom prostrate willingly without the prostration being burdensome to them, and some of whom find it burdensome, because committing to the obligation is hardship, yet they bear the hardship out of sincerity and faith, until they become accustomed to the truth and practise it. The second approach, which is the sound one, is to apply the verse generally. On this there are two ways. The first is that the believer prostrates willingly, while the disbeliever is commanded to prostrate and is held accountable for it. The second, which is the truth, is that the believer prostrates with his body willingly, and every created being, whether believer or disbeliever, prostrates by virtue of being created: it prostrates as an indication of, and a need for, the Maker. This is like His saying: ﴿And there is not a thing but glorifies His praise﴾ [al-Isra': 44], which is glorification as indication, not glorification as worship.

(﴿And their shadows, in the mornings and the evenings﴾) That is, the shadows of created things prostrate to Allah, the Exalted, in the mornings and the evenings, because they become apparent at these two times and incline from one side to another; this is Allah's disposing of them as He wills. It is like His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Have they not seen what things Allah has created, whose shadows incline from the right and the left, prostrating to Allah while they are humbled?﴾ [al-Nahl: 48]. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and others. Mujahid said: the shadow of the believer prostrates willingly while it is obedient, and the shadow of the disbeliever prostrates unwillingly while it is unwilling. Ibn al-Anbari said: the shadows are given intellects by which they prostrate and humble themselves, just as the mountains were given understanding so that they addressed and were addressed. Al-Qushayri said: there is room for scrutiny in this, for the mountain is a substance, so it is possible for it to have intellect on the condition of assuming life for it, whereas shadows are accidents and attributes, and it is not conceivable to assume life for them. Prostration means inclination, so the prostration of shadows is their inclining from side to side. It is said: "sajadat al-nakhlah," meaning the palm tree inclined.

Al-Asal is the plural of asul, and asul is the plural of asil, which is the period between the afternoon prayer and sunset; then asa'il is the plural of the plural. Abu Dhu'ayb al-Hudhali said:

"By my life, you are the house; I honour its people,
and I sit in its shade in the evenings."

Wa-zilaluhum may be coordinated with "man" (in the preceding phrase), and it may be in the nominative as the subject of a nominal sentence, with the predicate omitted; the sense being: "and their shadows are prostrating in the mornings and the evenings." "Bil-ghuduw" may be a verbal noun, and it may be the plural of ghadah; the fact that it is a plural is reinforced by its being set against the plural al-asal, which is paired with it.

The commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 13, verse 16:

God's words: ﴿Say: Who is the Lord of the heavens and the earth?﴾ God commanded His Prophet (ﷺ) to say to the polytheists: "Say: Who is the Lord of the heavens and the earth?" Then He commanded him to say to them [to them] [[من اووو ح.]]: "It is God," as a way of binding them with the proof, if they do not say so and are ignorant of who He is.

(Say: Have you then taken, besides Him, protectors?) This indicates that they acknowledge that God is the Creator, [and otherwise] the argument "Say: Have you then taken, besides Him, protectors?" would have no meaning. Its evidence is His words: ﴿And if you ask them who created the heavens and the earth, they will surely say, "God."﴾ [Az-Zumar: 38] That is: once you have acknowledged this, why do you worship other than Him? That other cannot benefit or harm, and this is a sound argument. [See vol. 15, p. 358.] Then He set forth a parable for them, saying: (Say: Are the blind and the seeing equal?) So likewise, the believer who sees the truth is not equal to the polytheist who does not see the truth. It is also said: the blind man is a parable for what they worship besides God, and the seeing one is a parable for God, Exalted is He. (Or are the darkness and the light equal?) That is, polytheism and faith.

Ibn Muhaysin, Abu Bakr, al-A'mash, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "yastawī" with the *yā'* (يسوي) because the verb is placed before its subject, and because the feminine marking of "al-zulumat" is not real (not a true feminine). The rest read it with the *tā'* (تستوي), and Abu 'Ubayd preferred this reading, saying: "because no barrier has come between the feminine noun and the verb." "Al-zulumat wa-l-nur" is a parable of faith and unbelief, and we do not know the precise manner of this.

(Or have they set up for God partners who have created as He created, so that the creation seemed alike to them?) This is part of the argument: that is, something other than God created like His creation, so the creation seemed alike to them, and they could not tell God's creation from the creation of their gods.

(Say: God is the Creator of all things.) That is: say to them, O Muhammad: "God is the Creator of all things," and it follows from this that everything must worship Him. This verse is a refutation of the polytheists and of the Qadariyya (those who deny divine decree and predestination), who claimed that they create just as God creates.

(And He is the One, the Subduer.) The One before everything. "Al-Qahhar" (the Subduer) is the Overpowering over everything, who prevails in His will over every one who wills. Al-Qushayri Abu Nasr said: It is not far-fetched that the verse is addressed to one who does not acknowledge the Maker. That is, ask them about the Creator of the heavens and the earth, for it is easy to establish the proof against them in this, and the matter approaches what is self-evident, since the incapacity of inanimate things and of every created being to create the heavens and the earth is known. Once this is established, and it becomes clear that the Maker is God, how is it permissible to count a partner with Him? In the course of the discourse he also made clear that if the world had two makers, the creation would be confused, and the act of one would not be distinguished from the act of the other. So how could it be known that the act comes from two?!

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 13 (al-Ra'd), verses 17–19:**

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿He sends down water from the sky, and the valleys flow according to their capacity, and the torrent carries a foaming scum.﴾ This is a parable (*mathal*) struck for truth and falsehood. He likened disbelief to the scum that rises upon water. It dissipates and clings to the sides of the valleys, and the winds drive it away. Likewise, disbelief departs and vanishes, as we will explain.

Mujahid said: "﴿and the valleys flow according to their capacity﴾" means according to their fullness. Ibn Jurayj said: according to their smallness and their greatness. Al-Ashhab al-'Uqayli and al-Hasan read "*bi-qadrihā*" with a sukun on the *dal*, and the meaning is the same. It has also been said that its meaning is "according to what was decreed for them." *Al-awdiyah* is the plural of *al-wadi* (valley). It was named *wadi* because of its flowing out and its running, so on this understanding *al-wadi* is a name for the flowing water.

Abu 'Ali said: "﴿the valleys flow﴾" is a case of *tawassu'* (figurative extension of language), meaning that its water flowed, and the word for water was elided. He said: the meaning of "*bi-qadarihā*" is according to the quantity of their waters, because the valleys do not flow according to their own size. "﴿The torrent carries a foaming scum﴾" means a scum that is high, elevated, and raised above the water. The sentence is complete here, as Mujahid said.

Then He says: (and from what they kindle over fire) — this is the second parable.

(seeking ornament) means the ornament of gold and silver.

(or goods, a scum like it). Mujahid said: this refers to iron, copper, and lead. The phrase "*zabadun mithluhu*" means that a scum rises over these substances just as it rises over the torrent. The torrent carried scum only because the earth's soil mixed with the water, and this became scum. Likewise, what is kindled in the fire of precious substances, gold and silver, and other metals scattered in the earth, has been mixed with soil. It is kindled only so that it melts and the soil of the earth separates from it.

And His saying: (So Allah strikes the parables of truth and falsehood. As for the scum, it passes away as refuse) — Mujahid said: "*judha'an*" means dried up and hardened. Abu 'Ubaydah said, quoting Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala': *ajfa'at al-qidr* means the cooking pot boiled until its foam was poured out, and when it hardened at its bottom. *Al-juf'* is what the valley casts away, that is, what it throws out. Abu 'Ubaydah related that he heard Ru'bah recite "*judhalan*," and Abu 'Ubaydah said: it is said *ajfalat al-qidr* when it throws out its foam, and *ajfalat al-rih al-sahab* when the wind scatters the clouds.

(And as for what benefits people, it remains in the earth). Mujahid said: this is pure, clear water. It has also been said: this refers to water and what is purified of gold, silver, iron, copper, and lead. The two parables were struck by Allah for truth in its stability and for falsehood in its dissolution. Falsehood, even if it rises in some circumstances, will vanish as scum and dross vanish. It has also been said: the intended meaning is a parable Allah struck for the Qur'an and what enters hearts from it. He likened the Qur'an to rain for the generality of its benefit and the lasting of its good, and He likened hearts to valleys, into which the Qur'an enters in proportion to their breadth and narrowness.

Ibn 'Abbas said: "﴿He sends down water from the sky﴾" means the Qur'an. "﴿The valleys flow according to their capacity﴾" means the valleys are the hearts of the servants.

The author of *Suq al-'Arus* [[This is Abu Ma'shar 'Abd al-Karim ibn 'Abd al-Samad al-Tabari, who settled in Makkah and died there in the year 478 AH. His book *Suq al-'Arus* concerns the sciences of the Qira'at (recitations).

(Kashf al-Zunun).]] said: if this exegesis is sound, then its meaning is that Allah the Exalted likened the Qur'an to water, likened hearts to valleys, likened the muhkam (clear, definitive verses) to the clear water, and likened the mutashabih (ambiguous verses) to the scum. It has also been said: the scum is the stirrings of the soul and the perils of doubt, which rise from within it and are agitated by the power of its surface, just as the torrent's water flows clear and lifts whatever it finds remaining in the valley. As for the ornament of gold and silver, it is like the noble states and the pure character traits by which men are beautified and righteous deeds are sustained, just as gold and silver are the adornment of women and by them the value of things is measured.

Humayd, Ibn Muhaysin, Yahya, al-A'mash, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Hafs read "*yūqidūna*" with the *ya'* (third person). Abu 'Ubayd preferred this reading because of the phrase "*yanfa'u al-nas*," which is in the third person, and there is no direct address here. The rest read it with the *ta'* (second person), in agreement with His saying at the beginning of the passage: ﴿Have you taken protectors other than Him?﴾ [Al-Ra'd: 16].

His saying "*fi al-nar*" (in the fire) is connected to an omitted element and is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*). The one it describes is the *ha'* in "*'alayhi*" (upon it). The sense is: "and from what you kindle upon it while it is established in the fire, or while it is existing." In His saying "*fi al-nar*" there is a pronoun in the nominative that refers back to the *ha'*, which is the subject of the circumstantial clause. It is not correct to connect "*fi al-nar*" to "*yūqidūna*," because one does not say *awqadtu 'alayhi fi al-nar* (I kindled upon it in the fire), since the thing kindled upon is necessarily in the fire, and then "*fi al-nar*" would become unrestricted.

His saying "*ibtigha'a hilyah*" is an object of purpose (*maf'ul lahu*). "*Zabadun mithluhu*" is a subject and predicate, meaning: a scum like the scum of the torrent. It has also been said that the predicate of "*zabad*" is His saying "*fi al-nar*." Al-Kisa'i said: "*zabad*" is the subject, "*mithluhu*" is its adjective, and the predicate lies in the sentence before it, which is "*mimma yūqidūna*" (from what they kindle).

(Thus Allah strikes the parables) means: just as He has explained these parables to you, so He strikes them clearly. The sentence is complete here. Then He says: (for those who respond to their Lord) — that is, they answered. *Istajaba* has the same meaning as *ajaba*. [[This is Ka'b ibn Sa'd al-Ghanawi, lamenting his brother Abu al-Mighwar. The first half of the line is:

"And a caller called, 'O you who answers to generosity.'"]]:

"But no answerer answered him at that time."

This has already been mentioned. It means they responded to what Allah called them to, namely monotheism and prophethood.

(the best reward) because it is at the utmost of goodness. It has also been said that among "*al-husna*" is victory in this world and everlasting bliss tomorrow.

(And those who do not respond to Him) means they did not answer the call to faith in Him.

(Even if they had all that is in the earth, and the like of it with it) means wealth that belongs to them.

(they would ransom themselves with it) from the punishment of the Day of Resurrection. Its parallel in Al 'Imran is: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve, their wealth and their children will never avail them against Allah at all﴾ [Al 'Imran: 10], and ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve and die while they are disbelievers, never will be accepted from any of them the earth filled with gold, even if they should ransom themselves thereby﴾ [Al 'Imran: 91], according to what was explained there before. [[See vol. 4, p. 21 onward.]]

(For them is the evil of the reckoning) means that no good deed of theirs will be accepted, and no evil deed of theirs will be overlooked. Furqad al-Sabakhi [[Al-Sabakhi: (with two fatha) attributed to al-Sabakhah, a place in Basra.]] said: Ibrahim al-Nakha'i said to me: "O Furqad! Do you know what the evil of the reckoning is?" I said: "No." He said: "It is that a man is called to account for all his sins, and nothing of them is forgiven him."

(Their refuge is Hell) meaning their dwelling and their place of abode.

(and what an evil resting place) meaning the bed they prepared for themselves.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Is one who knows that what has been revealed to you from your Lord is the truth equal to one who is blind?﴾ This is a parable Allah struck for the believer and the disbeliever. It is related that it was revealed about Hamzah ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib, may Allah be pleased with him, and Abu Jahl, may Allah curse him. The blindness intended is blindness of the heart, and the one ignorant of the religion is blind of heart.

(Only the people of understanding remember).
