**Two issues arise here.** The first is His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Those who fulfil the covenant of God﴾. This is a description of people of understanding (dhawu al-albab), meaning that only those of understanding who fulfil the covenant of God are the ones who take heed. The word "covenant" (ʿahd) is a generic noun, so it refers to all of God's covenants, which are His commands and prohibitions that He enjoined upon His servants. Included in these words is the commitment to all obligations and the avoidance of all sins. His statement, "and they do not break the compact" (wa-la yanquduna al-mithaq), may mean the genus of compacts: if they bind themselves to a covenant in obedience to God, they do not break it. Qatadah said: "God laid down to His servants the prohibition against breaking the compact and forbade it in some twenty verses." It may also refer to a specific compact, namely the one God took from His servants when He brought them forth from the loins of their father Adam. al-Qaffal said: it is what was implanted in their intellects of the proofs of monotheism (tawhid) and prophethood.

The second issue: Abu Dawud and others related from Awf ibn Malik, who said: "We were with the Messenger of God (ﷺ), seven or eight or nine of us, and he said: 'Will you not pledge allegiance to the Messenger of God (ﷺ)?' We had only recently pledged allegiance (in the previous one)." [In manuscript "wāw": "bay'atihi" (his allegiance).] "So we said: 'We have already pledged allegiance to you,' until he said it three times. Then we extended our hands and pledged allegiance to him. One of them said: 'O Messenger of God! We have already pledged allegiance to you, so upon what shall we pledge allegiance to you?'" [The addition is from the books of hadith.] He said: "That you worship God, associate nothing with Him, perform the five prayers, listen and obey"—and he whispered a hidden word—"and that you do not ask people for anything." He said: "Indeed, some of those men would drop their whip and would not ask anyone to hand it to them."

Ibn al-ʿArabi said: Among the greatest covenants in remembrance is that one should not ask anyone other than Him. Abu Hamzah al-Khurasani was one of the great worshippers. He heard that some people had pledged allegiance to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) not to ask anyone for anything, and the hadith continues. Abu Hamzah said: "My Lord! These people pledged to Your Prophet when they saw him, and I pledge to You that I will not ask anyone for anything." He said: He set out on pilgrimage from Syria, intending Mecca. While he was walking on the road at night, he fell behind his companions for some excuse, and then he went after them. While he was walking to catch up with them, he fell into a well beside the road. When he settled at its bottom, he said: "I will call for help, perhaps someone will hear me." Then he said: "The One to whom I pledged will see me and hear me. By God! I will not speak a word to a human being." Then he waited only a little while when a group of people passed by that well. When they saw him at the side of the road, they said: "It is fitting to seal up this well." They then cut wood, set it over the mouth of the well, and covered it with dust. When Abu Hamzah saw this, he said: "This is destruction!" Then he wanted to call out to them, but he said: "By God! I will never come out of it." Then he returned to himself and said: "Did you not pledge to the One who sees you?" So he fell silent and placed his trust (tawakkul) in God. Then he leaned at the bottom of the well, reflecting on his situation. Suddenly the dust was falling upon him and the wood was being lifted from him. In the midst of that, he heard someone saying: "Give me your hand!" He said: "I gave him my hand, and he lifted me in one go to the mouth of the well. I came out, but I did not see anyone. Then I heard a voice saying: 'How did you find the fruit of tawakkul?'" And he recited:

*Modesty before You prevented me from uncovering my desire,*
*so You enriched me with knowledge of You from uncovering it.*

*You were gentle in my affair, and You displayed my witness*
*to my absent one, and gentleness is perceived by gentleness.*

*You revealed Yourself to me with knowledge, until it is as though*
*You inform me of the unseen that You are in the palm of my hand.*

*I see myself, and in me from my awe of You is a loneliness,*
*so You make me intimate with gentleness from You and with tenderness.*

*You give life to a lover whose death is in love with You,*
*and it is strange: how can there be life along with death?*

Ibn al-ʿArabi said: This is a man who pledged to God and found fulfilment in full and complete measure, so follow him, God willing, and you will be guided.

Abu al-Faraj al-Jawzi said: This man's silence in this situation, on the pretext of tawakkul, was in fact an aid against himself, and that is not permissible. Had he understood the meaning of tawakkul, he would have known that it does not contradict seeking help in that situation, just as the Messenger of God (ﷺ) did not depart from tawakkul by concealing his departure from Mecca, by hiring a guide, by keeping that matter secret, by hiding in the cave, and by his saying to Suraqah: "Conceal this from us." Praiseworthy tawakkul is not attained through a forbidden act, and the silence of this man who fell into the well was forbidden to him. The explanation is that God has created for the human being an instrument by which he averts harm and an instrument by which he attracts benefit. If he disables them while claiming tawakkul, that is ignorance of tawakkul and a rejection of the wisdom of humility, because tawakkul is only the heart's reliance upon God, and it does not require abandoning means. If a person went hungry and did not ask until he died, he would enter the Fire, as Sufyan al-Thawri and others said, because he had been shown the path to safety, and if he neglects it he aids himself against himself.

Abu al-Faraj also said: No attention should be paid to Abu Hamzah's statement, "Then a lion came and brought me out," for even if that is authentic, such a thing may happen by chance, or it may be a kindness from God to the ignorant servant. It is not denied that God was gracious to him; what is denied is his act, which is his own acquisition (kasb), namely his aiding himself against his self, which is a trust (wadiʿah) from God with Him, and He has commanded him to guard it.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 13, verse 21–24:

His words, exalted is He: ﴿And those who join what Allah has commanded to be joined﴾ are apparent regarding the joining of the ties of kinship (silat al-arham). This is the view of Qatadah and most of the exegetes. Yet, despite this, it encompasses all acts of obedience.

(And they fear their Lord) It was said: regarding severing the ties of kinship. And it was said: regarding all acts of disobedience.

(And they fear the evil of the reckoning). The evil of the reckoning is scrutinizing it thoroughly and being called to account for every detail (al-munaqashah), and whoever has his reckoning scrutinized is punished. Ibn 'Abbas and Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: the meaning of "those who join what Allah has commanded to be joined" is belief in all the Books and all the Messengers. Al-Hasan said: it is joining with Muhammad ﷺ. It may also admit a fourth meaning: that they join faith with righteous deeds; "and they fear their Lord" in what He commanded them to join; "and they fear the evil of the reckoning" for neglecting it. The first view encompasses these sayings as we have mentioned, and with Allah is our success.

His words, exalted is He: ﴿And those who are patient, seeking the countenance of their Lord﴾ It was said: "those who" is a new (independent) clause, because "sabaru" is in the past tense and so it cannot be conjoined to "yufun" (they fulfil). It was also said: it is a description of those mentioned earlier. It is permissible to describe with the past form at one time and with the future form at another, since the meaning is "whoever does such-and-such, for him is such-and-such." Since "alladhina" (those who) implies a condition, and the past in a condition is like the future, this is permissible. For this reason He said: "those who fulfil", then said: "and those who are patient", then conjoined to it: "and they repel evil with good." Ibn Zayd said: they were patient in obedience to Allah, and patient in refraining from disobedience to Allah. 'Ata' said: they were patient under calamities, afflictions, misfortunes and trials. Abu 'Imran al-Jawni said: they were patient in their religion, seeking the countenance of Allah.

(And they establish the prayer) they performed it with its obligations and its humility at its appointed times.

(And they spend of what We have provided for them, secretly and openly) meaning the obligatory zakah, according to Ibn 'Abbas. The discussion of this has already passed in al-Baqarah [see vol. 1, p. 179] and elsewhere.

(And they repel evil with good) i.e., they repel the evil of deeds with righteous deeds. This is said by Ibn 'Abbas. Ibn Zayd: they repel evil with good. Sa'id ibn Jubayr: they repel wrongdoing with what is right. Al-Dahhak: they repel obscenity with greeting. Juwaybir: they repel injustice with pardon. Ibn Shajarah: they repel sin with repentance. Al-Qutabi: they repel the folly of the ignorant with forbearance; so folly is the evil and forbearance is the good. It was also said: when they intend an evil, they turn back from it and seek forgiveness. It was also said: they repel shirk with the testimony that there is no god but Allah. These are nine sayings, whose meanings are all close to one another, and the first encompasses them all generally. A parallel to this is: ﴿Indeed, good deeds remove evil deeds﴾ [Hud: 114]. And from it is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ to Mu'adh: "Follow the evil deed with a good deed and it will wipe it out, and treat people with good character."

His words, exalted is He: ﴿Those will have the good outcome of the home﴾, i.e., the final consequence of the Hereafter, which is Paradise in place of the Fire. The home tomorrow is of two abodes: Paradise for the obedient and the Fire for the disobedient. So when He mentioned the description of the obedient, their abode is inevitably Paradise. It was also said: by "the home" is meant the abode of this world, i.e., they will have the reward of the acts of obedience they performed in the abode of this world.

His words, exalted is He: ﴿Gardens of perpetual residence, which they will enter﴾, i.e., for them are Gardens of Eden. "Gardens of Eden" is a substitute (badal) for "outcome", and it is permissible that it be an explanation of "the good outcome of the home", meaning for them is the entry into Gardens of Eden, because "outcome of the home" is an event (hadath) and "Gardens of Eden" is a concrete entity ('ayn), and an event is only explained by a similar event; so the omitted verbal noun is idafah to its object. It is also permissible that "Gardens of Eden" be the predicate of an omitted subject. "Gardens of Eden" is the middle of Paradise and its center, and its ceiling is the Throne of the Merciful. Al-Qushayri Abu Nasr 'Abd al-Malik said: In Sahih al-Bukhari: "When you ask Allah, ask Him for al-Firdaws, for it is the middle and highest of Paradise, above it is the Throne of the Merciful, and from it the rivers of Paradise gush forth." So "Gardens" may be like this, if it is authentic, and that is a predicate. 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr said: In Paradise there is a palace called 'Adn, around it are towers and meadows, and in it are a thousand doors, on each door five thousand striped Yemeni garments (hibarah), and no one enters it except a prophet, a truthful one (siddiq), or a martyr. "Adn" is derived from 'adana bi-al-makan, when one dwells in a place, as will be explained in surah al-Kahf, if Allah wills.

(And whoever is righteous among their fathers, their spouses and their offspring) It may be conjoined to "those", meaning: those and whoever is righteous among their fathers, spouses and offspring will have the good outcome of the home. It may also be conjoined to the pronoun of subject in "they enter it", and the conjunction is acceptable since the object pronoun intervened between them. It may also mean: they enter it, and whoever is righteous among their fathers enters it too, i.e., whoever was righteous, not entering by lineage. It may also be that the position of "man" is accusative, under the assumption: they enter it together with whoever is righteous among their fathers, and even if he did not do deeds like theirs, Allah will join him to them as an honour to them. Ibn 'Abbas said: this righteousness is faith in Allah and the Messenger; and if along with faith they had other acts of obedience, they would enter by their obedience, not by way of following. Al-Qushayri said: there is room for examination in this, since faith is indispensable, so the view on the condition of righteous deeds is like the view on the condition of faith. The more apparent is that this righteousness is among the totality of deeds, and the meaning is that the blessing tomorrow is completed for them by Allah gathering them together with their relatives in Paradise, even though each person enters by his own deeds, but rather by the mercy of Allah, exalted is He.

His words, exalted is He: ﴿And the angels will enter upon them from every gate﴾, i.e., with gifts and presents from Allah, as an honour to them.

(Peace be upon you) i.e., they say: "Peace be upon you", so the verb is omitted, meaning: you have been safe from afflictions and trials. His words, exalted is He: ﴿Those will have the good outcome of the home﴾, i.e., the final consequence of the Hereafter, which is Paradise in place of the Fire. The home tomorrow is of two abodes: Paradise for the obedient and the Fire for the disobedient. So when He mentioned the description of the obedient, their abode is inevitably Paradise. It was also said: by "the home" is meant the abode of this world, i.e., they will have the reward of the acts of obedience they performed in the abode of this world.

His words, exalted is He: ﴿Gardens of perpetual residence, which they will enter﴾, i.e., for them are Gardens of Eden. "Gardens of Eden" is a substitute (badal) for "outcome", and it is permissible that it be an explanation of "the good outcome of the home", meaning for them is the entry into Gardens of Eden, because "outcome of the home" is an event (hadath) and "Gardens of Eden" is a concrete entity ('ayn), and an event is only explained by a similar event; so the omitted verbal noun is idafah to its object. It is also permissible that "Gardens of Eden" be the predicate of an omitted subject. "Gardens of Eden" is the middle of Paradise and its center, and its ceiling is the Throne of the Merciful. Al-Qushayri Abu Nasr 'Abd al-Malik said: In Sahih al-Bukhari: "When you ask Allah, ask Him for al-Firdaws, for it is the middle and highest of Paradise, above it is the Throne of the Merciful, and from it the rivers of Paradise gush forth." So "Gardens" may be like this, if it is authentic, and that is a predicate. 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr said: In Paradise there is a palace called 'Adn, around it are towers and meadows, and in it are a thousand doors, on each door five thousand striped Yemeni garments (hibarah), and no one enters it except a prophet, a truthful one (siddiq), or a martyr. "Adn" is derived from 'adana bi-al-makan, when one dwells in a place, as will be explained in surah al-Kahf, if Allah wills.

(And whoever is righteous among their fathers, their spouses and their offspring) It may be conjoined to "those", meaning: those and whoever is righteous among their fathers, spouses and offspring will have the good outcome of the home. It may also be conjoined to the pronoun of subject in "they enter it", and the conjunction is acceptable since the object pronoun intervened between them. It may also mean: they enter it, and whoever is righteous among their fathers enters it too, i.e., whoever was righteous, not entering by lineage. It may also be that the position of "man" is accusative, under the assumption: they enter it together with whoever is righteous among their fathers, and even if he did not do deeds like theirs, Allah will join him to them as an honour to them. Ibn 'Abbas said: this righteousness is faith in Allah and the Messenger; and if along with faith they had other acts of obedience, they would enter by their obedience, not by way of following. Al-Qushayri said: there is room for examination in this, since faith is indispensable, so the view on the condition of righteous deeds is like the view on the condition of faith. The more apparent is that this righteousness is among the totality of deeds, and the meaning is that the blessing tomorrow is completed for them by Allah gathering them together with their relatives in Paradise, even though each person enters by his own deeds, but rather by the mercy of Allah, exalted is He.

His words, exalted is He: ﴿And the angels will enter upon them from every gate﴾, i.e., with gifts and presents from Allah, as an honour to them.

(Peace be upon you) i.e., they say: "Peace be upon you", so the verb is omitted, meaning: you have been safe from afflictions and trials. It was also said: it is a supplication for them for the continuance of safety, even though they are already safe; i.e., may Allah keep you safe. So it is a statement whose meaning is supplication, and it implies acknowledgment of servanthood.

(For what you patiently endured) i.e., for your patience, so "ma" with the verb is in the sense of a verbal noun, and the "ba" in "bi-ma" is connected to the meaning of "Peace be upon you". It is also permissible that it be connected to an omitted element, i.e., this honour is for your patience, i.e., in obeying the command of Allah and refraining from His prohibition, as said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr. It was also said: for patience in poverty in the world, as said by Abu 'Imran al-Jawni. It was also said: for striving in the way of Allah, as narrated from 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Do you know who among Allah's creatures will enter Paradise?" They said: "Allah and His Messenger know best." He said: "The strivers (mujahidun) by whom the frontiers are guarded and by whom hardships are averted, so that one of them dies while his need is in his heart, unable to fulfil it; then the angels come to them and enter upon them from every gate: 'Peace be upon you for what you patiently endured; how excellent is the good outcome of the home.'" Muhammad ibn Ibrahim said: "The Prophet ﷺ used to visit the graves of the martyrs at the head of every year and say: 'Peace be upon you for what you patiently endured; how excellent is the good outcome of the home.'" Likewise Abu Bakr, 'Umar and 'Uthman. Al-Bayhaqi mentioned it from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Prophet ﷺ used to come to the martyrs, and when he came to the mouth of the valley (farhat al-sha'b) [the mouth of the ravine; the shi'b is the gap between two mountains, and the martyrs were at Mount Uhud] he would say: "Peace be upon you for what you patiently endured; how excellent is the good outcome of the home." Then Abu Bakr after the Prophet ﷺ did the same, and 'Umar after Abu Bakr did the same, and 'Uthman after 'Umar did the same. Al-Hasan al-Basri, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "For what you patiently endured" refers to patience concerning the superfluities of the world. It was also said: "For what you patiently endured" refers to persistence in obedience and abstaining from disobedience; this was said by al-Fudayl ibn 'Iyad. Ibn Zayd: "For what you patiently endured" refers to patience regarding what you love when you lose it. It is also possible, as a seventh view, that "for what you patiently endured" refers to restraint from following desires. It is narrated from 'Abdullah ibn Salam and 'Ali ibn al-Husayn, may Allah be pleased with them, that they said: When the Day of Resurrection comes, a caller will call: "Let the people of patience stand up." Some people will stand and be told: "Go to Paradise." The angels will meet them and say: "Where to?" They will say: "To Paradise." They will say: "Before the reckoning?" They will say: "Yes!" They will ask: "Who are you?" They will say: "We are the people of patience." They will ask: "What was your patience?" They will say: "We made ourselves patient in obedience to Allah, we made ourselves patient in refraining from the disobedience of Allah, and we made ourselves patient under afflictions and trials in the world." 'Ali ibn al-Husayn said: The angels will say to them: "Enter Paradise; how excellent is the reward of those who work." Ibn Salam said: The angels will say to them: "Peace be upon you for what you patiently endured; how excellent is the good outcome of the home," meaning: how excellent is the final outcome of the abode in which you were, the deeds you did in it which brought you to what you are in now. So "the outcome" according to this is a noun, and "the home" is this world. Abu 'Imran al-Jawni said: "How excellent is the good outcome of the home" is Paradise, away from the Fire. And from him: "How excellent is the good outcome of the home" is Paradise, away from the world.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (*al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran*) on surah 13, verses 25–26:

God's words: ﴿And those who break the covenant of God after its binding﴾. When He mentioned those who fulfil His covenant and maintain what He commanded, and what they receive, He mentioned their opposites. Breaking the covenant (*naqd al-mithaq*) means abandoning His command. It was also said: it means neglecting their intellects, so that they do not reflect with them in order to know God, exalted is He.

(And they sever what God has commanded to be joined): that is, of the ties of kinship, and belief in all the prophets.

(And they cause corruption on the earth): that is, through disbelief and the committing of sins.

(For them is the curse): that is, expulsion and removal from mercy.

(And for them is the evil abode): that is, the evil return, which is Jahannam (Hell). Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas said: "By God, other than whom there is no god, they are the Harurites (*al-Harurriyya*)."

God's words: ﴿God extends provision to whom He wills and restricts it﴾. When He mentioned the end of the believer and the end of the polytheist, He made clear that He is the One who extends provision and restricts it in this world, because this world is a place of trial. Therefore the extension of provision to the disbeliever does not indicate his honour, and the restriction of provision upon some believers does not indicate their humiliation. (*Yaqdiru*, "restricts"): that is, narrows. From this is ﴿And whoever has his provision restricted﴾ [al-Talaq: 7], that is, narrowed. It was also said: *yaqdiru* means He gives in measure sufficient for need.

(And they rejoiced in the life of this world): meaning the polytheists of Makkah. They rejoiced in the world and knew nothing else, and were ignorant of what is with God. This is coordinated with (And they cause corruption on the earth). In the verse there is inversion of order; the intended sense is: "And those who break the covenant of God after its binding, and sever what God has commanded to be joined, and cause corruption on the earth, and rejoice in the life of this world."

(And the life of this world, in comparison with the Hereafter): that is, in relation to it.

(is nothing but a provision): that is, a provision among provisions, like the bowl and the small dish. [Editor's note: *al-sukurruja* is a small vessel in which a little condiment is eaten; it is Persian in origin.] Mujahid said: a little thing that passes away, from *mut'u al-nahar*, when the day rises, so it must necessarily cease. Ibn Abbas said: a provision like the provision of a shepherd. It was also said: the enjoyment of the life of this world is what is enjoyed from it. It was also said: it is what one takes as provision from it for the Hereafter, of piety and righteous deeds. ﴿And for them is the evil abode﴾, then a new statement begins: ﴿God extends provision to whom He wills and restricts it﴾, that is, He expands and narrows it.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 13, verse 27–28:

His saying, Exalted is He: (And those who disbelieve say, "Why has not a sign been sent down to him from his Lord?") He explained in several places that demanding signs from the messengers is ignorance, after they had already seen one sign that indicates the truth. The one who said this was Abd Allah ibn Abi Umayya and his companions, when they demanded signs from the Prophet ﷺ.

(Say, "Indeed, Allah") Mighty and Majestic is He, (sends astray whom He wills), meaning: just as He misguided you after the signs He had sent down and deprived you of reflecting upon them, He will misguide you when other signs descend.

(And guides to Himself whoever turns back in repentance), meaning whoever returns. The pronoun in "ilayhi" refers to the Truth, or to Islam, or to Allah Mighty and Majestic, with the implied sense: and He guides to His religion and obedience whoever returns to Him in his heart. It has also been said that it refers to the Prophet ﷺ.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Those who believe﴾. "Alladhina" is in the accusative position, as it is the object, meaning: Allah guides those who believe. It has also been said that it is a substitute (badal) for the phrase "man anab," so it is likewise in the accusative position.

(And their hearts find rest in the remembrance of Allah), meaning they are calmed and find comfort in the oneness of Allah, so they become tranquil. He said: meaning their hearts are continually at rest through remembering Allah with their tongues; this was said by Qatadah. Mujahid, Qatadah and others said: through the Qur'an. Sufyan ibn Uyayna said: through His command. Muqatil said: through His promise. Ibn Abbas said: through swearing by His name; or their hearts find rest through remembering His grace and bounty, just as they are struck with fear through remembering His justice, His retribution and His decree. It has also been said: "through the remembrance of Allah" means they remember Allah and contemplate His signs, so they recognize the perfection of His power with insight.

(Unquestionably, through the remembrance of Allah do hearts find rest), meaning the hearts of the believers. Ibn Abbas said: this refers to oath-taking; when an opponent swears by Allah, his heart is at peace. It has also been said: "through the remembrance of Allah" means through obedience to Allah. It has also been said: through the reward of Allah. It has also been said: through the promise of Allah. Mujahid said: they are the companions of the Prophet ﷺ.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 13, verse 29:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Those who believe and do righteous deeds, for them is ṭūbā (blessedness)﴾. It is a mubtada' (subject) and its khabar (predicate). It was also said: its meaning is "for them is ṭūbā," so "ṭūbā" is marfū' (nominative) by being the subject. Its position may also be manṣūb (accusative), on the assumption: "He made for them ṭūbā." And "wa-ḥusnu ma'āb" (and a good place of return) is conjoined to it on both of the mentioned views, so it is either raised or put in the accusative. ʿAbd al-Razzaq related: Maʿmar informed us, from Yaḥyā ibn Abī Kathīr, from ʿAmr ibn Abī Yazīd al-Bikālī, from ʿUtba ibn ʿAbd al-Sulamī, who said: A bedouin came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and asked him about Paradise, and mentioned the Basin (al-ḥawḍ). He said: "Does it have fruit?" He said: "Yes, a tree called Ṭūbā." He said: "O Messenger of Allah! What tree of our land does it resemble?" He said: "It does not resemble any tree of your land. Have you come to Syria? There is a tree there called al-Jawza, which grows on a single trunk and whose top spreads out." He said: "O Messenger of Allah! How great is its root?" He said: "If you were to travel with a young she-camel of your family's camels, you would not get around its root until its collarbone was broken with age." And he mentioned the hadith, and we have written it in full in the chapter on the gates of Paradise in the book "al-Tadhkira," and praise be to Allah.

Ibn al-Mubarak also related: Maʿmar informed us, from al-Ashʿath, from ʿAbd Allah, from Shahr ibn Ḥawshab, from Abu Hurayra, who said: "In Paradise there is a tree called Ṭūbā. Allah, exalted is He, says to it: 'Burst open for My servant with whatever he wishes.' So it bursts open for him with a horse with its saddle, bridle and equipment, as he wishes, and it bursts open with a riding camel with its saddle-bags, its halter and its equipment, as he wishes, and with fine camels and garments."

Ibn Wahb also related, from the hadith of Shahr ibn Ḥawshab, from Abu Umama al-Bahili, who said: "Ṭūbā" is a tree in Paradise; there is no house in it except that a branch of it is in it, no beautiful bird except that it is in it, and no fruit except that it is of it.

It has been said: its root is in the palace of the Prophet (ﷺ) in Paradise, then its branches spread out among the dwellings of the people of Paradise, just as knowledge and faith have spread from him to all the people of the world. Ibn ʿAbbas said: "Ṭūbā lahum" means joy for them and coolness of the eye. It is also related from him that "Ṭūbā" is the name of Paradise in Abyssinian (Ethiopic). Saʿid ibn Jubayr and al-Rabiʿ ibn Anas said: it is the garden (al-bustān) in the language of India. Al-Qushayri said: If this is sound, then it is agreement between the two languages. Qatada said: "Ṭūbā lahum" means "good fortune (ḥusnā) for them." Ikrima said: "bounty (nuʿmā) for them." Ibrahim al-Nakhaʿi said: "good for them." And also from him: "honour from Allah for them." al-Daḥḥak said: "envy-worthy (ghibṭa) for them."

Al-Nahhas said: These sayings are close in meaning, because ṭūbā is fuʿlā from al-ṭayyib (the good), meaning a good life for them, and all these things return to the good thing. Al-Zajjaj said: ṭūbā is fuʿlā from al-ṭayyib, and it is the pleasant state for them. The original is ṭuybā, and the yāʾ became wāw because it is sukūn and the letter before it is ḍamma, as they say: mūsir and mūqin.

I say: The correct view is that it is a tree, because of the marfūʿ hadith we have mentioned. It is sound, as al-Suhayli mentioned; Abu ʿUmar mentioned it in al-Tamhid, and we have quoted from it. Al-Tha'labi also mentioned it in his tafsir. Al-Mahdawi and al-Qushayri also mentioned, from Muʿawiya ibn Qurra, from his father, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Ṭūbā is a tree in Paradise which Allah planted with His own hand and breathed into it of His spirit. It produces ornaments and garments, and its branches are visible from behind the wall of Paradise." Whoever wishes more than these reports should consult al-Tha'labi.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: "Ṭūbā" is a tree in Paradise whose root is in the house of ʿAli, and in the house of every believer there is a branch of it. Abu Jaʿfar Muhammad ibn ʿAli said: The Prophet (ﷺ) was asked about the saying of Allah, exalted is He: "Ṭūbā lahum wa-ḥusnu ma'āb," and he said: "A tree whose root is in my house and whose branches are in Paradise." Then he was asked about it again and said: "A tree whose root is in the house of ʿAli and whose branches are in Paradise." It was said to him: "O Messenger of Allah! You were asked about it and you said, 'Its root is in my house and its branches are in Paradise,' then you were asked about it and said, 'Its root is in the house of ʿAli and its branches are in Paradise.'" The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "My house and the house of ʿAli tomorrow in Paradise are one, in one place."

Also from him (ﷺ): "It is a tree whose root is in my house, and there is no house among your houses except that a branch of it hangs down into it."

(And ḥusnu ma'āb) — āba means "he returned." It was also said: the sense of the statement is: "Those who believe, whose hearts are at rest through the remembrance of Allah, and who do righteous deeds, for them is ṭūbā."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 13, verse 30:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Thus We have sent you to a community before which other communities have passed away﴾, i.e., We have sent you just as We sent the prophets before you. This is what al-Hasan said. It was also said: He likened the favour bestowed upon those to whom Muhammad, peace be upon him, was sent to the favour bestowed upon those to whom the prophets before him were sent.

(﴿That you may recite to them that which We have revealed to you﴾) meaning the Qur'an.

(﴿while they disbelieve in the Most Merciful﴾) Muqatil and Ibn Jurayj said: It was revealed concerning the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah, when they wanted to write the document of the treaty. The Prophet ﷺ said to Ali: "Write: In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate." Suhayl ibn Amr and the polytheists said: "We do not know the Merciful except the Lord of al-Yamamah," meaning Musaylimah the liar. "Write: In Your name, O Allah," and this is how the people of the Jahiliyyah used to write. The Prophet ﷺ then said to Ali: "Write: This is what Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah, has agreed to." The polytheists of Quraysh said: "If you were the Messenger of Allah, we would not have fought you and barred you; we would have wronged you. Rather, write: This is what Muhammad ibn Abd Allah has agreed to." The companions of the Prophet ﷺ said: "Let us fight them." He said: "No, but write what they desire." So it was revealed. Ibn Abbas said: It was revealed concerning the disbelievers of Quraysh when the Prophet ﷺ said to them: ﴿Prostrate to the Most Merciful﴾ [al-Furqan: 60], and they said: "And what is the Most Merciful?" Then it was revealed.[[See vol. 10, p. 342.]]

(﴿Say﴾) to them, O Muhammad: the One whom you denied.

(﴿He is my Lord; there is no deity but Him﴾) and there is no worshipped one besides Him. He is One in His essence, even though the names of His attributes differ.

(﴿Upon Him I have relied﴾) and I have depended upon Him and trusted Him.

(﴿And to Him is my return﴾) i.e., my place of return tomorrow; and today as well, upon Him I rely and trust, being content with His decree and submitting to His command. It was also said: Abu Jahl heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ supplicating in al-Hijr, saying: "O Allah, O Merciful," and he said: "Muhammad forbids us from worshipping the gods, yet he calls upon two gods." So this verse was revealed, and there was also revealed: ﴿Say: Call upon Allah or call upon the Most Merciful﴾ [al-Isra': 110].[[See vol. 13, p. 64.]]

The Qur'anic verse here is connected to the statement: ﴿Why has no sign been sent down to him from his Lord?﴾ [Yunus: 20]. The reason for its revelation is that a group of the polytheists of Makkah, among them Abu Jahl and Abdullah ibn Abi Umayya al-Makhzumi, sat behind the Ka'bah. Then they sent for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he came to them. Abdullah said to him: "If it pleases you that we follow you, then make the mountains of Makkah move for us through the Qur'an, and remove them from us until the land opens up, for it is a narrow land. Make for us rivers and springs within it, so that we may plant and sow. You are not, as you claim, more honored with your Lord than Dawud, for whom the mountains were subjected to move with him. Subject the wind for us so that we may ride it to al-Sham, carrying our goods and needs there, and return the same day. Sulayman was given control over the wind, as you claim, so you are not more honored with your Lord than Sulayman ibn Dawud. Bring back to life for us Qusayy (he is Qusayy ibn Kilab), your grandfather, or whoever you wish from among our dead, and we will ask him whether what you say is true or false. Isa used to raise the dead, and you are not more honored with Allah than he is." Then Allah revealed: ﴿And if a Qur'an had been such that mountains could be moved by it...﴾. This is said by al-Zubayr ibn al-Awwam, Mujahid, Qatadah and al-Dahhak. The answer (jawab) is omitted, its estimated form being: "this Qur'an would have been [the one that moves them]." It is omitted for brevity, because the meaning is indicated by the apparent words, as Imru' al-Qays said:

"Had it been a soul that dies all at once...
but it is a soul that falls away, soul by soul."

He means: it would have been easy for me. This is the meaning of the statement of Qatadah, who said: "If a Qur'an other than yours had done this, your Qur'an would have done it." His words "yaysiruni min ayasar al-jazur" mean "they cut me up and divide me", and he mentioned this because he had been taken captive, and they cast lots over him with arrows of the maysir, reckoning the division of his ransom.]

I say to them at the ravine when they cast lots over me,
"Have you not known that I am the son of Fares Zahdam?"

"Have the peoples not known that I am his son,

"He consumed my old wealth and what I had gathered of property,

That is, the disbelievers will not cease to be struck by a destructive calamity: a thunderbolt as struck Arbad, or killing, or captivity, or drought, or other punishments and afflictions, as befell the mockers, who were the leaders of the polytheists. (Or it descends) i.e., the calamity descends (close to their homes). This is said by Qatadah and al-Hasan. Ibn Abbas said: "Or you descend close to their homes." (So how was My punishment?) That is: how did you see what I did to them? Likewise I shall do to the polytheists of your people.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿For them is a punishment in the life of this world.﴾ That is, for the polytheists who bar [others], by killing, captivity, imprisonment, and other things: sicknesses and calamities.

(And the punishment of the Hereafter is harder.) That is, more severe, from your saying: "shaqqa 'alayya kadha, yashuqqu" (it was hard upon me).

(And they have no protector from Allah.) That is, no one who prevents them from His punishment, nor any defender. And "min" is superfluous.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 13, verse 35:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The parable of the Garden which the God-fearing have been promised﴾. The grammarians differed over the case of "mathal" (parable). Sibawayh said: it is in the nominative by being a subject (mubtada', inchoative), and its predicate is omitted; the implied meaning is: "And in what is recited to you is the parable of the Garden." Al-Khalil said: it is in the nominative by being a subject, and its predicate is "flowing beneath it are rivers," meaning: the description of the Garden which the God-fearing have been promised is that rivers flow beneath it, just as your saying "my saying is: Zayd stands" — "my saying" is the subject and "Zayd stands" is its predicate. The use of "mathal" in the sense of "description" is attested. God exalted says: ﴿That is their parable in the Torah, and their parable in the Gospel﴾ [al-Fath: 29], and He says: ﴿And to God belongs the highest parable﴾ [al-Nahl: 60], meaning the highest attribute.[[See vol. 16, p. 192.]][[See vol. 10, p. 119.]] Abu 'Ali denied this and said: "mathal" has not been heard in the sense of "attribute"; its meaning is "likeness" (shabah). Do you not see that it takes its place in its contexts and derivations, as when they say: "I passed by a man like you (mathalaka)," just as you say: "I passed by a man like you (shabahaka)." He said: It is also corrupt from the standpoint of meaning, because if "mathal" meant "attribute," the sentence would be: "the attribute of the Garden in which are rivers," and that is not sound, for the rivers are in the Garden itself, not its attribute. Al-Zajjaj said: God, mighty and majestic, has presented to us what is hidden from us by what we see, and the meaning is: the parable of the Garden is a garden beneath which rivers flow. Abu 'Ali denied this too, saying: on his view "mathal" must be either "attribute" or "likeness," and on both readings what he said is not valid. If it means "attribute," it is invalid, because when you say "the attribute of the Garden is a garden," making "the Garden" the predicate, it is not sound, since the Garden cannot be the attribute. Likewise, "the likeness of the Garden is a garden" is not sound either. Do you not see that "likeness" is an expression for the resemblance between two things that resemble each other, which is an event (hadath), whereas the Garden is not an event, so the first cannot be the second. Al-Farra' said: "mathal" is inserted for emphasis, and the meaning is: "The Garden which the God-fearing have been promised, beneath which rivers flow." The Arabs often do this with "mathal," as in His saying: ﴿There is nothing like unto Him﴾ [al-Shura: 11], meaning: "There is nothing like Him."[[See vol. 16, p. 8.]] [[In manuscript ī: "laysa kahu" (not "laysa kamithlihi") noted as variant.]] It has also been said that the implied meaning is: the description of the Garden which the God-fearing have been promised is the description of a garden beneath which rivers flow. It has also been said that the meaning is: the likeness of the Garden which the God-fearing have been promised, in beauty, blessing and eternity, is like the likeness of the Fire in punishment, severity and eternity; this was said by Muqatil.

﴿Its fruit is everlasting﴾: it does not cease. In a report it is said: "When a fruit is taken, another grows in its place." We have explained this in "al-Tadhkira."

﴿And its shade﴾: that is, and its shade is likewise everlasting, the verb being omitted: its fruit does not cease and its shade does not pass away. This is a refutation of the Jahmiyya, in their claim that the bliss of Paradise passes away and perishes.

﴿That is the final outcome of those who guarded (against evil), and the final outcome of the disbelievers is the Fire﴾: that is, the end of the deniers and their final abode is the Fire, into which they will enter.

﴿And those to whom We gave the Book rejoice at what has been sent down to you﴾. That is, some of those who were given the Book rejoice in the Qur'an, such as Ibn Salam (ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam) and Salman, and those who came from Abyssinia. The wording is general, but the intended meaning is specific. Qatadah said: "They are the Companions of Muhammad (ﷺ), who rejoice in the light of the Qur'an." Mujahid and Ibn Zayd also said this. It is also reported from Mujahid that they are the believers among the People of the Book. It was said: they are the whole body of People of the Book, Jews and Christians, who rejoice at the sending down of the Qur'an because it confirms their Books. Most of the scholars said: mention of "the Merciful" (al-Rahman) in the Qur'an was rare at the beginning of the revelation. When ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam and his companions embraced Islam, they were troubled by the scarcity of the mention of "the Merciful" in the Qur'an, given how often it is mentioned in the Torah. So they asked the Prophet about this, and Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿Say: Call upon Allah, or call upon the Merciful; whichever you call upon, to Him belong the most beautiful names﴾ [al-Isra' 17:110]. The Quraysh then said: "What is wrong with Muhammad? He used to call to one God, and now he calls upon two gods, Allah and the Merciful! By Allah, we know of no Merciful except the Merciful of Yamamah," meaning Musaylimah the Liar. So the verse was revealed: ﴿And they disbelieve in the remembrance of the Merciful﴾ [al-Anbiya' 21:36], and ﴿while they disbelieve in the Merciful﴾ [al-Ra'd 13:30]. Then the believers among the People of the Book rejoiced at the mention of the Merciful, and Allah the Exalted revealed: "And those to whom We gave the Book rejoice at what has been sent down to you."

(﴿And among the factions﴾) means the polytheists of Makkah, and those among the Jews, Christians and Magians who did not believe. It was also said: they are the Arabs who banded together against the Prophet (ﷺ). It was said: among the enemies of the Muslims are those who deny some of what is in the Qur'an, because among them were some who acknowledged some of the prophets, and some who acknowledged that Allah is the Creator of the heavens and the earth.

(﴿Say: I have only been commanded to worship Allah and not to associate anything with Him﴾). The recitation of the majority is with the accusative (naṣb), as a conjunction (ʿaṭf) on "aʿbud" (I worship). Abu Khalid [in some manuscripts: Abu Khulayd, who is ʿUtbah ibn Hammad al-Hukmi, and who transmitted from Nafiʿ; see Ghayat al-Nihayah] read it in the nominative (rafʿ) as a resumptive sentence (isti'naf, a new independent clause), meaning: I single Him out for worship alone, with no partner, and I disavow the polytheists, and whoever says: the Messiah is the son of Allah, and ʿUzayr is the son of Allah, and whoever holds the belief in anthropomorphism, like the Jews.

(﴿To Him I call﴾), that is, I call people to His worship.

(﴿And to Him is my return﴾), that is, I turn back to Him in all my affairs.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 13, verse 37:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And thus We have sent it down as an Arabic judgment﴾, meaning: just as We sent down the Qur'an to you, and some of the factions denied it, so We sent it down as an Arabic judgment. He described it thus because He sent it down upon Muhammad (ﷺ), who is an Arab, and the factions denied this judgment too. It was also said that the structure of the verse is: just as We sent the Books to the Messengers in their languages, so We sent down to you the Qur'an as an Arabic judgment, i.e., in the tongue of the Arabs. By "judgment" is meant what it contains of rulings. It was also said: by the "Arabic judgment" he meant the whole Qur'an, because it distinguishes between truth and falsehood and passes judgment.

﴿And if you were to follow their desires﴾, meaning the desires of the polytheists in worshipping what is other than Allah and in turning toward other than the Ka'bah (qibla),

﴿after the knowledge that has come to you, you would have no protector from Allah, nor any shield﴾, meaning: no helper who would help you.

﴿nor any shield﴾ that would protect you from His punishment. The address is to the Prophet (ﷺ), and what is meant is the Community (ummah).

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 13, verse 38:

There are two issues in this.

The first: It is said that the Jews criticized the Prophet ﷺ for having wives, and they reproached him for this, saying: "We do not see this man having any concern except women and marriage. If he were a prophet, the matter of prophethood would have occupied him away from women." So Allah revealed this verse, and reminded them of the matter of Dawud and Sulayman, saying: ﴿And We had certainly sent messengers before you and made for them wives and descendants﴾. That is, We made them human beings who fulfill what Allah has permitted of the desires of this world. The specialness lies only in the revelation.

The second: This verse indicates encouragement toward marriage and urging upon it, and it forbids tabattul (ascetic abstention from marriage), which is leaving marriage. This is the practice of the messengers, as this verse explicitly states, and the Sunnah has come with its meaning. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Marry, for I will boast of you before the nations," and the hadith continues. It has already been mentioned in "Al 'Imran" [[See vol. 4, p. 72 onwards.]]. He also said: "Whoever marries has completed half of the religion, so let him fear Allah regarding the other half" [[Ibn al-Jawzi narrated in al-'Ilal: "Whoever marries has secured half of his religion, so let him fear Allah regarding the remaining half." See the hadith with its chains in vol. 2 of Kashf al-Khafa, p. 239, where there is discussion.]]. The meaning of this is that marriage guards one from fornication, and chastity is one of the two qualities for which the Messenger of Allah ﷺ guaranteed Paradise, saying: "Whoever is protected by Allah from the evil of two things, enters Paradise: what is between his jaws and what is between his legs." Al-Muwatta' and others recorded it. In Sahih al-Bukhari, on the authority of Anas, who said: "Three men came to the houses of the wives of the Prophet ﷺ asking about the worship of the Prophet ﷺ. When they were informed, they seemed to consider it little, and they said: 'Where are we in relation to the Prophet ﷺ! Allah has forgiven him what preceded of his sin and what followed.' One of them said: 'As for me, I will pray at night forever.' Another said: 'I will fast the entire year and not break it.' And another said: 'I will keep away from women and never marry.' Then the Messenger of Allah ﷺ came to them and said: 'Are you the ones who said such and such? By Allah, I am the most fearful of Allah among you and the most mindful of Him, but I fast and break my fast, I pray and I sleep, and I marry women. Whoever turns away from my Sunnah is not of me.'" Muslim recorded it with a similar meaning, and this is clearer. In Sahih Muslim, on the authority of Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, who said: "'Uthman wished to abstain (from marriage), and the Prophet ﷺ forbade him. Had he permitted him to do so, we would have castrated ourselves." It has already been mentioned in "Al 'Imran" [[See vol. 4, p. 72, and vol. 6, p. 260 onwards.]] the urging to seek offspring and the refutation of one who is ignorant of this. It is also narrated from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, that he used to say: "I marry a woman though I have no need for her, and I have intercourse with her though I have no desire for her." It was said to him: "What drives you to this, O Commander of the Faithful?" He said: "My love that Allah bring forth from me one whom the Prophet ﷺ will boast of over the prophets on the Day of Resurrection. I heard him say: 'Upon you is (marriage to) virgins, for they are sweeter in speech, better in character, and more fertile in wombs, and I will boast of you before the nations on the Day of Resurrection.'" By "more fertile in wombs" he means "more receptive to offspring." A woman who has many children is called natiq, because she casts out children abundantly (rami'). Abu Dawud recorded on the authority of Ma'qil ibn Yasar, who said: A man came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and said: "I have found a woman of noble lineage and beauty, but she cannot bear children. Shall I marry her?" He said: "No." Then he came to him a second time, and he forbade him. Then he came to him a third time, and he said: "Marry the loving and the fertile, for I will boast of you before the nations." Abu Muhammad 'Abd al-Haqq declared it sound, and that is sufficient for you.

His saying the Exalted: ﴿It was not for a messenger to bring a sign except by permission of Allah﴾. The discourse returns to what they proposed of the signs, which were mentioned earlier in this surah. So Allah revealed that concerning them. The apparent wording is a prohibition, but its meaning is negation, because one is not prohibited from something he has no power over.

(﴿For every term is a decree﴾) That is, for every matter that Allah has decreed there is a book with Allah. Al-Hasan said this. It was also said that there is inversion in it; the meaning is: for every book there is a term. Al-Farra' and al-Dahhak said: for every matter that Allah has written there is a fixed term and a known time. Its parallel is: ﴿For every news there is a fixed time﴾ [[See vol. 7, p. 11.]] [al-An'am: 67], which shows that the intended meaning is not in accordance with the peoples' proposals for the descent of punishment, but rather for every term there is a book. It was also said: the meaning is that for every period there is a written book and a decree that the angels do not comprehend. Al-Tirmidhi al-Hakim mentioned in "Nawadir al-Usul," on the authority of Shahr ibn Hawshab, on the authority of Abu Hurayra, who said: When Musa, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him, ascended Mount Sinai, he saw the Tyrant with a ring on his finger. He said: "O Musa, what is this?" – though He knew best about it. He said: "A piece of men's adornment." He said: "Is there written on it any of My names or My speech?" He said: "No." He said: "Then inscribe on it: 'For every term there is a book.'"

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 13, verse 39:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Allah effaces what He wills and establishes [what He wills]﴾. That is, He erases from that Book whatever He wills to bring about for its people and whatever He wills to bring. "And establishes" [what He wills], that is, He postpones it until its appointed time. It is said: "I erased the writing (maḥawtu al-kitāba) with erasure (maḥwan)," meaning I removed its trace. "And establishes" means "and establishes it," as in His saying: ﴿And the men who remember Allah much and the women who remember [Him]﴾ [al-Ahzab: 35], meaning "and the women who remember Allah." [See vol. 14, p. 185.]

Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and 'Asim read "wa-yuthbit" with a light (unshaddated) *th*, while the rest read it with a doubled (shaddated) *th*. The reading of Ibn 'Abbas, and the preference of Abu Hatim and Abu 'Ubayd, is [the form with the doubled letter] because of the number of those who recite it that way, and because of His saying: ﴿Allah makes firm those who believe﴾ [Ibrahim: 27]. [See p. 362 of this volume.]

Ibn 'Umar said: I heard the Prophet (ﷺ) say: "Allah effaces what He wills and establishes, except happiness, misery, and death."

Ibn 'Abbas said: "Allah effaces what He wills and establishes, except for several things": creation, character, the term of life, provision, happiness, and misery. He also said: "There are two books besides the Mother of the Book; Allah effaces from them what He wills and establishes."

﴿And with Him is the Mother of the Book﴾: the one in which nothing is ever changed. Al-Qushayri said: It has also been said that happiness, misery, creation, character, and provision do not change, so the verse refers to things other than these. In this view there is a kind of arbitrariness. I say: Such matters are not known through opinion and personal reasoning (ra'y and ijtihad); they are taken only from revealed authority (tawqif). If it is authentic, then it must be affirmed and one must stop at it. Otherwise, the verse is general in regard to all things, and this is the more apparent view, and Allah knows best. Its meaning is also transmitted from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, and Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Wa'il, Ka'b al-Ahbar, and others, and it is the view of al-Kalbi.

It is related from Abu 'Uthman al-Nahdi that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, used to circumambulate the House while weeping and saying: "O Allah, if You have written me among the people of happiness, then keep me among them; and if You have written me among the people of misery and sin, then efface me and write me among the people of happiness and forgiveness, for You efface what You will and establish, and with You is the Mother of the Book."

Ibn Mas'ud said: "O Allah, if You have written me among the fortunate, then keep me among them; and if You have written me among the wretched, then efface me from the wretched and write me among the fortunate, for You efface what You will and establish, and with You is the Mother of the Book."

Abu Wa'il used to supplicate often: "O Allah, if You have written us as wretched, then efface [that] and write us as fortunate; and if You have written us as fortunate, then keep us [so], for You efface what You will and establish, and with You is the Mother of the Book."

Ka'b said to 'Umar ibn al-Khattab: "Were it not for a verse in the Book of Allah, I would inform you of what will happen until the Day of Resurrection." [He meant] "Allah effaces what He wills and establishes, and with Him is the Mother of the Book."

Malik ibn Dinar, concerning a woman for whom he prayed, said: "O Allah, if there is a girl in her womb, then change it to a boy, for You efface what You will and establish, and with You is the Mother of the Book."

It has already been mentioned in the two Sahihs (of al-Bukhari and Muslim) from Abu Hurayrah, who said: I heard the Prophet (ﷺ) say: "Whoever would be pleased that his provision be expanded and his *athar* be delayed, let him maintain the ties of kinship." [Note: *al-athar* means the term of life; it is so called because it follows the lifespan. Its root is the trace of one's footsteps on the earth; when a person dies, no trace remains and no mark of his feet is seen on the ground.]

Similarly from Anas ibn Malik, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever loves..." and he mentioned it with the same wording. In it there are two interpretations. The first is figurative: what remains after him of good praise, good remembrance, and continuing reward, so that it is as though he has not died. The second: his appointed term, written in the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh al-mahfuz), is delayed, while what is in Allah's knowledge is fixed and unchangeable, as He said: "Allah effaces what He wills and establishes, and with Him is the Mother of the Book."

When Ibn 'Abbas was told of the authentic hadith from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he said: "Whoever wishes that Allah extend his life and his term, and expand his provision, let him fear Allah and maintain the ties of kinship," [the question was raised:] "How can life and term be increased?!" He said: Allah, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿It is He who created you from clay, then decreed a term; and a specified term is with Him﴾ [al-An'am: 2]. The first term is the servant's lifespan from the time of his birth until his death, and the second term, the one "specified with Him," is from the time of his death until the day he meets [Allah] in the barzakh (the intermediate realm), which no one knows except Allah. So when the servant fears his Lord and maintains the ties of kinship, Allah increases for him, from the barzakh term, whatever He wills, within the first term of his life. And when he disobeys and severs his ties of kinship, Allah reduces from the term of his life in this world whatever He wills, and so He adds to his term in the barzakh. When the term is fixed in His prior knowledge, increase and decrease become impossible, as He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿When their term comes, they cannot delay it an hour, nor can they advance it﴾ [al-A'raf: 34]. Thus the report and the verse agree. This is an increase in the very lifespan and the term itself according to the apparent meaning of the wording, according to the view of the scholar of the Ummah (Ibn 'Abbas), and Allah knows best. [See vol. 6, p. 387.]

Mujahid said: Allah decrees the matter of the year during Ramadan, so He effaces what He wills and establishes what He wills, except life and death, and misery and happiness. The discussion of this has already passed.

Al-Dahhak said: Allah effaces from the register of the guardian angels whatever has in it neither reward nor punishment, and establishes whatever has in it reward and punishment. Abu Salih related its meaning from Ibn 'Abbas.

Al-Kalbi said: He effaces from provision and adds to it, and He effaces from the term and adds to it; and he related this from the Prophet (ﷺ). Then al-Kalbi was asked about this verse, and he said: Everything is written down, until when Thursday comes, everything in it that has neither reward nor punishment is cast out, such as your saying: "I ate, I drank, I entered, I went out," and similar things, though it is true; and what has in it reward and punishment is established.

Qatadah, Ibn Zayd, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: Allah effaces what He wills of the obligatory (*fara'id*) and voluntary (*nawafil*) [acts], abrogating and replacing them, and establishes what He wills so that it is not abrogated. The whole of the abrogating and the abrogated is with Him in the Mother of the Book. Similar to this is what al-Nahhas and al-Mahdawi related from Ibn 'Abbas. Al-Nahhas said: Bakr ibn Sahl related to us, saying: Abu Salih related to us, from Mu'awiyah ibn Salih, from 'Ali ibn Abi Talhah, from Ibn 'Abbas: "Allah effaces what He wills" means: Allah replaces from the Qur'an what He wills, abrogating it; "and establishes" what He wills, so He does not replace it; "and with Him is the Mother of the Book" means: all of that is with Him in the Mother of the Book, the abrogating and the abrogated.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr also said: He forgives what He wills, that is, of the sins of His servants, and leaves what He wills so He does not forgive it.

'Ikrimah said: He effaces what He wills, meaning through repentance, all sins, and establishes in place of sins good deeds; [Allah said]: ﴿except for one who repents, believes, and does righteous work﴾ [al-Furqan: 70], the verse. [The bracketed words are supplied from *al-Bahr al-Muhit*.] [See vol. 13, p. 77.]

Al-Hasan said: "Allah effaces what He wills": [this means] whoever's term has come; "and establishes": whoever's term has not come. Al-Hasan also said: He effaces the fathers and establishes the sons. He also said: He causes the guardian angels to forget sins, yet He does not forget.

Al-Suddi said: "Allah effaces what He wills" means the moon, and "establishes" means the sun. Its explanation is His saying: ﴿So We effaced the sign of the night and made the sign of the day illuminating﴾ [al-Isra': 12]. [See vol. 10, p. 227.]

Al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: This concerns souls during sleep. He takes them at sleep; then, when He wills their death, He suddenly withholds them, and whomever He wills to continue, He establishes and returns to its owner. Its explanation is His saying: "Allah takes the souls at the time of their death" [al-Zumar: 42], the verse. [See vol. 15, p. 265 and p. 22.]

'Ali ibn Abi Talib said: "Allah effaces what He wills" from the generations, like His saying: ﴿Have they not seen how many generations We destroyed before them?﴾ [Ya-Sin: 31], "and establishes from them what He wills," like His saying: ﴿Then We produced after them another generation﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 31]. So He effaces one generation and establishes another.

It has also been said: [this refers to] a man who performs obedience to Allah for a long time and then acts in disobedience to Allah and dies upon his misguidance; he is the one who is effaced. And the one who is established is the man who acts in disobedience to Allah for a long time and then repents, so Allah effaces it from the register of evil deeds and establishes it in the register of good deeds. This was related by al-Tha'labi and al-Mawardi from Ibn 'Abbas.

It has also been said: "Allah effaces what He wills," meaning this world, "and establishes" the Hereafter.

Qays ibn 'Abbad said concerning the tenth day of Rajab: It is the day on which Allah effaces what He wills and establishes what He wills. It has already been mentioned from Mujahid that this occurs in Ramadan.

Ibn 'Abbas said: Indeed Allah has a Preserved Tablet, the distance of five hundred years' travel, made of white pearl, with two covers of red ruby. Allah looks into it three hundred and sixty times each day; He establishes what He wills and effaces what He wills. [Variant: "from" (min).]

Abu al-Darda' related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Indeed Allah, glorified is He, opens the Book of Remembrance during the last three hours of the night, and He looks into the Book which no one else looks into, and He establishes what He wills and effaces what He wills."

The creed is that there is no alteration of Allah's decree. This effacing and establishing is among what was preceded by the decree. It has already been mentioned that among the decree is what occurs as a fixed and inevitable matter, and this is the established; and among it is what is diverted by causes, and this is the effaced. And Allah knows best.

Al-Ghaznawi said: In my view, what is on the Tablet has come out of the unseen by the awareness of some angels, so it is open to alteration, because the creation's comprehension of all of Allah's knowledge is impossible; but what is in His knowledge of the determination of things is not changed.

"And with Him is the Mother of the Book": the origin of what was written of terms and other things. It has also been said: The Mother of the Book is the Preserved Tablet, which is not altered or changed. It has also been said: Alteration does occur in it. And it has been said: It occurs only in the other registers.

Ibn 'Abbas was asked about the Mother of the Book, and he said: It is Allah's knowledge of what He will create and what His creatures will do. He said to His knowledge: "Be a book," and there is no alteration in Allah's knowledge. And it is related from him that it is the Reminder (*al-dhikr*). Its evidence is His saying: ﴿And We wrote in the Psalms after the Reminder﴾ [al-Anbiya': 105]. [See vol. 11, p. 349.] This meaning returns to the first, and it is the meaning of Ka'b's statement.

Ka'b al-Ahbar said: The Mother of the Book is Allah's knowledge of what He has created and what He will create.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 13, verses 40–41:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Whether We show you some of what We promise them﴾ (wa-in ma nuriyannaka ba'da alladhi na'iduhum). "Ma" is superfluous (za'idah), and the sense is: "And if We show you some of what We promise them", meaning of the punishment, in accordance with His saying: ﴿For them is a punishment in the life of this world﴾ [al-Ra'd: 34] and His saying: ﴿And disaster will not cease to strike those who disbelieve because of what they have done﴾ [al-Ra'd: 31]. That is: if We show you some of what We have promised them, ﴿or We take you (in death), then upon you is only the delivery (of the message)﴾. So there is upon you nothing but the delivery (al-balagh), that is, the conveying (al-tabligh), ﴿and upon Us is the reckoning﴾, that is, the recompense and the punishment.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Do they not see﴾, meaning the people of Makkah, ﴿that We come to the land﴾, that is, We intend it.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 13, verse 42–43:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And those before them had already schemed﴾, meaning: before the idolaters of Makkah. They schemed against the messengers, plotted against them, and disbelieved in them.

(﴿To Allah belongs all scheming﴾), meaning: the scheming of schemers is a creation of His; it does not harm except by His permission. It was also said: "To Allah belongs the best of scheming," meaning He will requite them for it.

(﴿And the disbelievers will know﴾). This is the reading of Nafi', Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr. The rest read "al-kuffar" (the disbelievers) in the plural. It was also said that what is meant by it is Abu Jahl.

(﴿to whom belongs the final outcome of the abode﴾), meaning the final outcome of the abode of this world in reward and punishment, or: to whom belongs reward and punishment in the Hereafter. This is a threat and a warning.

(﴿Say: Allah suffices as a witness﴾), meaning: say to them, O Muhammad, "Allah suffices as a witness", i.e., Allah suffices (﴿as a witness between me and you﴾) concerning my truthfulness and your lying.

(﴿and whoever has knowledge of the Book﴾). This is an argument against the idolaters of the Arabs, because they used to refer to the People of the Book, those of them who believed, regarding the explanations (tafasir). It was also said: their testimony was decisive against the claims of the adversaries, and they are the believers among the People of the Book, such as 'Abd Allah ibn Salam, Salman al-Farisi, Tamim al-Dari, al-Najashi and his companions. Al-Tirmidhi narrated from the nephew of 'Abd Allah ibn Salam, who said: When [the killing of] 'Uthman was intended, 'Abd Allah ibn Salam came, and 'Uthman said to him: "What brought you?" He said: "I came to support you." He said: "Go out to the people and drive them away from me, for your going out is better for me than your coming in." [He said] So 'Abd Allah ibn Salam went out to the people and said: "O people! My name in the Jahiliyyah was so-and-so, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ named me 'Abd Allah, and verses of the Book of Allah were revealed concerning me: ﴿And a witness from among the Children of Israel testified to its like, and believed, while you were arrogant. Al-Qushayri said: Ibn Jubayr said the surah is Makkan, and Ibn Salam embraced Islam in Madinah after this surah, so this verse cannot be applied to Ibn Salam. Rather, "whoever has knowledge of the Book" is Jibril, and this is the saying of Ibn 'Abbas. Sulayman ibn Arqam narrated it from al-Zuhri from Salim from his father from the Prophet ﷺ. Mahbub narrated from Isma'il ibn Muhammad al-Yamani that he read it thus: "wa-min 'indihi" with kasra on the mim, 'ayn and dal, "'ulima al-kitabu" with damma on the 'ayn and raf' on al-kitab. He said: "Rather, it is 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him." Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyyah also said likewise. It was also said: it is all the believers, and Allah knows best. The judge Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi said: As for the one who said it is 'Ali, he relied on one of two aspects: either because he is the most knowledgeable of the believers, which is not so; rather Abu Bakr, 'Umar and 'Uthman are more knowledgeable than him. Ibn Taymiyyah affirmed that it was fabricated by the Shi'ah]. The Prophet ﷺ is the city of knowledge, and his companions are its gates; among them is the wide gate and among them the middling gate, according to their ranks in the sciences. As for the one who said they are all the believers, he spoke truly, for every believer knows the Book, perceives the aspect of its inimitability, and bears witness to the truthfulness of the Prophet ﷺ. I say: the Book in this view is the Qur'an. As for the one who said it is 'Abd Allah ibn Salam, he relied on the hadith of al-Tirmidhi. It is not impossible that a verse was revealed concerning 'Abd Allah ibn Salam while its wording encompasses all the believers, and the coherence of the passage supports this, since the saying of His exalted words "and those who disbelieve say" refers to Quraysh, so those who have knowledge of the Book are the believers among the Jews and Christians, who are closer to knowing prophethood and the Book than the worshippers of idols. Al-Nahhas said: the saying of the one who said it is 'Abd Allah ibn Salam and others is also possible, because when the proofs are sound and are recognized by one who has read the books revealed before the Qur'an, it is a matter of greater confirmation, and Allah knows best the reality of that.
